Steam communication during the year 1903, i.e., for not less than llfty-two full round weekly trips between St. John and Halifax, via Yarmouth and other wray ports, $10,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: There is an increase iu this vote of $3,000.
Yes; it is proposed to make this a weekly service. It used to be thirty-two trips a year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I suppose these vessels carry passengers and freight, as well as the malls 7
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Can the minister tell us whether there is an increase of trade and passenger traffic, and whether it looks as it this service would become self-sustaining?

I am rather afraid, judging from past experience, that it will he a good while before it will be self-sustaining. The trade is considerable, but, as reported to me, there does not appear to be any very considerable increase, except, perhaps, in the passenger traffic. The passenger traffic of late has increased a good deal, but not the amount of freight. On the other hand, these vessels have, as a rule, carried pretty good cargoes. They call at a considerable number of ports along that coast.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Why is it more necessary to subsidize a vessel running from one point to another on the Atlantic coast than it is from Kingston to Toronto on Lake Ontario 7

I have asked that question myself once or twice. It is to a considerable extent use and wont. I am inclined to think these services were inherited by us at confederation. Prior to confederation. I believe, the Nova Scotia government used

to subsidize most, but not all, the services for which we are now takiug' votes. Of course, the hon. gentleman is aware that a great many of these sections are very poorly supplied with railway accommodation as compared with other parts of the country. That no doubt is the case why subsidies were originally given, and also why the subsidies are now continued. But I do not know that there is any special reason why one should be subsidized more than the other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I do not think that is a very good reason. If my memory serves me right, the hon. gentleman used to condemn this expenditure in opposition.
No, I do not think I did.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
In the position the right hon. gentleman occupies now, if he finds there is an evil he should check it.
- The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE. I do not think the hon. gentleman will find that I voted to strike it out. Of course, if he thinks it is an improper expenditure, it is quite open to him to move to strike it out.
I do not say that. But as the hon. gentleman feels conscientious scruples about continuing it he ought to have backbone enough to strike it out himself.
But I did not vote against the subsidies.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I think if the Minister of Trade and Commerce opposed this in opposition, that is the best argument why it should be maintained at the present time. I want to tell the hon. gentleman and the people of Ontario especially, that we have no proper railway accommodation in Nova Scotia. In Nova Scotia we have only 900 miles of railway all told, and our province is two or three hundred years of age ; while in Manitoba, which is only of twenty-five or thirty years' growth, they have nearly 3,000 miles of railway. But the Minister of Trade and Commerce was so dominant in Ontario with a certain section of the people-I am bound to say it was a narrow section, such as the Postmaster General leads to-day-
The leadership has passed from the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

It was at any rate a narrow section of Ontario. But I find that to-day the belief is thoroughly grounded in the people of Ontario that Sir Charles Tup-per and the men we sent up here filled that province with railways and spent the money ef Canada for the benefit of the maritime provinces, whereas in Ontario they got no public expenditure at all. The fact is we have suffered in the maritime provinces to

build up the province of Ontario. But we did it uncomplainingly. We said to ourselves that surely the time would come when the people of Ontario would get generous and offer to give back to the people of Nova Scotia something to repay them for the great self-sacrifice they have made to build up the province of Ontario. But the time seems never to come ; and I want the people of Ontario on both sides of the House to understand that so far as railways are concerned, we are simply at the porch of the temple, we have not entered the temple of railway building in the province of Nova Scotia, and we blame that on the people of Ontario. Sir Charles Tupper, when he was here, endeavoured to give railroads, not only to Ontario and to the west, but to the maritime provinces ; but he found his own party first on his back, then he found the Liberals on his back, and he could not struggle up with both parties on his back. He could not liberalize both parties in the province of Ontario. The result was that in Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces we are without railways today. Therefore, we had to resort to these tu'penny ha'penny grants to run steamers around the shores of the province in order to give us communication. But these tu'penny ha'penny grants should be doubled or quadrupled in order to give some practical benefit to the commerce of the maritime provinces.
Steam eomunication between a port or ports in Prince Edward Island Jand a port or ports in Great Britain. $10,000.
What is the position of that communication at the present time ?

At present we are getting two trips, and we had a good deal of difficulty in getting vessels to call there. My hon. friends from Prince Edward Island have represented to me that it would be much more profitable for them if this vote was reduced and they obtained better communication with Nova Scotia. I am disposed to do that, and I only require for the service which is now under contract the sum of $5,000. Therefore, I move to reduce that vote to $5,000. But I may state that the sum so saved I propose to give, in the supplementary estimates, to another service for the benefit of the island.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Is this $10,000 to be appropriated for two trips only ?
I propose to appropriate $5,000 to the twe trips that I have contracted for.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Is it the intention of the minister to endeavour to obtain more service if possible ?
The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COM-
MERCE. If I could have obtained it I

would have retained the vote in its present shaptj.
The right hon. gentleman has not entirely given up the idea of trying to obtain a better service ?

No ; but for the present year I do not propose to deprive the island of the $5,000 ; I propose to apply it for its benefit in another service, which will be brought down in the supplementary estimates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Would, the right hon. gentleman state what service that will be ?
The service for which the balance will be appropriated will be between Prince Edward Island, Sydney and Newfoundland.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Has the right hon. minister any steamer to undertake that service ?
We are endeavouring to arrange for that at the present moment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Does the right: hon. minister know when the first trip will be made to the old country ?
We expect in October and that trips will also be made in November and December as may be found most convenient for the trade of the island.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: In what way is the $5,000 that is to be appropriated for some other service to be expended ?
In providing a service between Prince Edward Island, Sydney and Newfoundland.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Is there any steamer on that route at present or is one to be provided ?
One is to be provided.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What steamer do you propose to get for the service between Prince Edward Island, Sydney and Newfoundland?

We are negotiating for that, but we have not settled the matter yet.
Direct fortnightly steam service between Montreal, Quebec amd Manchester, England, during thp summer season, and between St. John. Halifax and Manchester during the winter season, $35,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What line receives this subsidy ?

The Manchester Line. The ships are known as the Manchester Line with various addenda, such as ' Manchester Liner,' 243
' Manchester Trader,' ' Manchester Commerce ' and names of that kind. The hon. gentleman, I suppose, is aware, that the reason why we have! been induced to take this up is that the corporation of Manchester has constructed a ship canal leading directly to the city of Manchester which is the centre, perhaps, of the very largest consuming population in England and we have deemed it expedient to endeavour to promote trade with Manchester. A very considerable trade has been developed, it is increasing and is likely to increase. The subsidy was formerly $38,000 and it has been reduced to $35,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Are these boats supplied with cold storage or cooled chambers ?
The MINISTER OF 'TRADE AND1 COMMERCE. Most of them are supplied with cold storage, but not all. I may also mention that these people have considerably exceeded their contract. They have given us more voyages than the contract called for. I think the chances are that the trade will not merely develop in a way that will make it a valuable trade for us, but if I am correctly advised the population around Manchester is so densed that within a circuit of between three and four miles there is now stated to be a population of nearly 8,000,000 people, almost all of whom are consumers and not producers of food stuffs; so that, if we can establish a trade proportionate to the consumption we will do very well.
Is there any stipulation in the contract requiring the vessels or any number of them to be supplied with cold storage ?

Most of them are. The corporation of Manchester, who, I understand, are largely concerned in these vessels have, as perhaps the hon. gentleman knows, warehouses especially adapted to the reception of food products in which everything can be placed immediately on arrival. My deputy tells me that he believes that all but two are supplied with the requisite cold storage accommodation.
Direct monthly steam communication between Canada and South Africa, $146,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: This we had under discussion some few weeks ago, as perhaps hon. gentlemen will remember, and I laid upon the Table the contract with the three firms who proposed to carry this on. Of course, nothing has been paid to them as yet. It depends entirely' on the vote of the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What ports will be called at ?
Cape Town, Durban and Port Elizabeth.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: And East London ?
We have the liberty of requiring them to call at three ports besides Cape Town.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: How many trips have been made already?

They commenced in October and they have made eight or nine trips, I think.
Mr. CLARKE, i Have the ships had any difficulty in getting cargoes both ways ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The chief complaint that has reached me as yet has been not so much on this side as on the other side. I have been in communication with parties in Natal in the endeavour to obtain better accommodation for our ships when they go there. They have complained that they were held over and found a good deal of difficulty and delay in discharging their cargoes. On the whole the cargoes have been pretty good.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: From where ?
From here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Do they get a return cargo ?
Not much. There is comparatively little at present to return to us from South Africa. It may improve.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: They come back in ballast ?

We do not interfere with their return voyage. It is their voyage to South Africa that we are concerned in. When they get to South Africa they have to find their way back, but they may go to England, Australia or elsewhere provided a vessel is1 forthcoming at the requisite time on our side of the ocean.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What do their cargoes from here consist of ?

We have sent lumber, agricultural implements, and we sent out what the Americans would call a cargo of notions on two or three occasions-furniture and miscellaneous articles of all sorts and descriptions. WTe have also been sending a good deal of flour and oats.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: How much flour has been sent ?
I am told that on several of their voyages the amount of flour sent was a couple of thousand tons, which is very good if it lasts.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Are the Canadian agents in Africa under the control of the department presided over by the fight hon. gentleman?
Yes, if Mr. Jardine is the gentleman referred to.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What does he do ?
His present office is to examine the general condition of the country and to report from time to time, and he has made ten or eleven reports to us
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Reports are easily made.

Yes. He has made these reports pointing out the articles that in his judgment can be most advantageously dealt with from Canada to South Africa. I might add that he has called attention to one feature of the trade which I hope will not need to be called attention to again, and that is the fact that goods forwarded to South Africa on two or three occasions have not been equal to the samples sent.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What kind of goods?

Articles like lumber. They did not equal the articles that had been ordered, and a good deal of trouble ensued in consequence. I need not say to the House that it is of the first importance, particularly when you are opening up a new trade, that the articles sent should at the very least equal the description. Nothing can do us more harm, in opening up new trade, than to let it be supposed that Canadian merchants will not live up to the samples they send, or will not attend to the orders that are given to them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: It would be advisable that the commercial agents for Canada, both in South Africa and Australia, should not only act as agents for the sale of Canadian goods, but should encourage the people of these countries to trade with us. I found in Australia and New Zealand very little interest in Canadian trade, because there was no market in Canada for any of their produce, which largely consists of hides and wool. If there was some interest on the part of the merchants there who have goods to sell in Canadian trade, it would be a great help to Canada.
Quite true. I have instructed them on that head.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I might point out that in Canada there are two firms that have taken first and second prizes in England for the manufacture of wind pumps.
What's that?

Wind pumps.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.
I have no doubt that Canada is well able to turn out wind pumps, as wind is at a premium. However, I have no reference to the Department of Agriculture.
I am not under lire to-day.
If our agent drew attention to this fact in South Africa, he would find a ready sale for these articles.
When was this South African subsidy first granted?
The first vote was $5,000 a couple of years a^o, but that was only for the purpose of getting a ship to make an experimental voyage, and I think lumber was chiefly carried.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The vote is now $146,000, and no doubt the Canadian people are anxious to get this trade if possible, but would the minister tell us why he recommended such a large expenditure and what is his anticipation of the future as to trade with South Africa.

This is to be regarded as an experiment, of course, but it was only found possible to obtain a regular monthly steamship service by offering pretty liberal treatment. From Montreal to Cape Town the distance is 6,500 miles, and to Durban it would be 1,000 miles further. We found it almost impossible to get any single company to undertake this service, and the contract is made in a somewhat unusual fashion, the Allans, the Elder-Dempster and the Furness-Withy lines each taking one-third. I placed the contract on the Table of the House a few weeks ago giving full details. How far it will succeed I cannot say as yet, but there is a very considerable industrial development going on in South Africa, particularly in the Transvaal, and the parts adjacent, and it is hoped that we will be able to supply them not merely with a very considerable amount of coarse goods, such as lumber, but food products of various kinds, and possibly furniture and agricultural implements.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Who is our chief competitor there ?

The United States have a pretty large trade there, and one chief reason for our establishing the service was the complaint made to us by Canadian merchants that their consignments were tossed to one side in New York, and that they had very little satisfaction in trading from that port. The various representatives of commerce throughout the country pressed on us rather 243i
strongly to give them a Canadian line, in which case they stated a very considerable trade would be developed. It is too early yet to judge, but I think there is a fair chance that a reasonable trade will be developed; I hope a large trade ultimately. The difficulty is that there is no large return cargo, and we are obliged to allow the various ships, if they cannot obtain cargo for Canada, to go around by England or elsewhere.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I am informed that so far the expectation of the government has not been realized, and that the trade during the eight months has not been up to expectations.

I cannot exactly say that. I did not expect myself that it could attain full grown proportions in the course of six months. You will have to nourish these infants a little before you can expect very much out of them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Is there any complaint from the shippers in respect to the freight rates?
There was some complaints six or seven months ago, but lately I am told that the service has been more satisfactory.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What was the complaint ?
The complaint was, in part, that the service was irregular, that they did not start on the day appointed, and that they attempted to obtain American trade in preference to Canadian.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Is not that the complaint at the present moment?

I am told that the present complaint has been made as to the matter of cold storage provided for in the contract; that an undue proportion of that has been assigned to American shippers. I called the attention of the various parties concerned to that, and I think if that has been the case heretofore it will be remedied now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I suppose that the anticipation of the government was that there would be some fruit trade developed between South Africa and Canada ?
No, I did not expect that there would be much of that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What is the cold storage for to which the hon. minister refers ?
This is for the benefit of Canadian products.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
I understand that there is a very serious complaint from the fruitgrowers of Canada that the vessels are not

fitted up in such a way tliat we might expect a trade between Canada and South Africa to develop.

The storage accommodation provided was, I think, intended, not so much for fruit, although that is, of course, an item that may be included, as for such articles as cheese, meat products and perhaps butter. If the hon. gentleman will look at the contract which has been laid on the Table, he will find the details there set out pretty fully.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Do we send butter to South Africa ?

We tried to do so, and were fairly successful. We send considerable cheese. Of course, these vessels have to cross the equator, where there is risk of injury to the products. I depend more upon cheese, meat products and canned products than upon such an article as butter. There is a pretty large demand in Johannesburg and all the adjacent regions of thel Rand. The American trade with them! amounts to a very considerable sum. That we hope to cut into.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I understand that these vessels carry American products as well as Canadian. Can the hon. gentleman tell us which are carried at the cheaper rate ?
The freight rate from New York is somewhat lower, I think, than ours, but not very much. That is scarcely to be avoided under the circumstances.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Do these vessels call at New York ?
No, they go straight to Cape Town, and then along the coast.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Do they come to our ports from New York ?

They are at liberty to go where they please on the return voyage. They may come from New York, but they do not take any freight from New York. They carry Canadian freight from the various ports between Montreal and Halifax.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: How many trips are made under this contract each year 1
There is one trip per month. We have the right to vary the ports from time to time, as we see fit.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: On the return voyage, the vessels could go to Buenos Ayres anti get wool or tallow and to Rio for coffee.
Yes, they may go where they please. There is at present scarcely any return freight from South Africa.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I observe that there is provision in the contract by which the government can establish a maximum of freight rates. Can the hon. gentleman tell whether or not any such schedule of rates has been established ?
Not as yet. We have been waiting to see how this trade developed before we attempted that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Does the hon. minister know whether the United States government pay any subsidy to vessels ?
I think they pay nothing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I understood the hon. minister to say that there had been some complaint with regard to the allotment to American shippers of too much cold storage accommodation. As a. matter of fact, is there any considerable quantity of produce shipped to the United States, by means of these lines ?

The hon. gentleman knows that the Canadian Pacific usually picks up a certain amount of American freight and takes it through to St. John. It has been from that quarter chiefly that any American produce has come.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Where does the Canadian agent make his headquarters ?

He has been travelling all over South Africa, from Cape Town to Pretoria and Johannesburg, with an excursion into Rhodesia. It is a pretty large country, and his instructions were in the first instance to make himself acquainted with the whole of the South African territory under British rule. He reports regularly to my department, and his reports are communicated to the various boards of trade and commerce.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What wages does he get ?
Two thousand dollars a year and his travelling expenses.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The minister speaks of the American traffic over this line as being largely by way of St. John ; that is to say, the shipments from Montreal and Quebec ?
I refer to what is carried in cold storage. I do not think there has been any large amount of the other kinds.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Could the minister give us any idea of what proportion of the carryings consist of United States produce and manufactures, and what proportion of Canadian produce and manufactures ?

With the exception of what is carried in cold storage, the percentage of American goods carried is very small. The great bulk has been Canadian goods, and our instructions, of course, were that Canadian goods should have the preference.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Of course, it might alter our ideas as to the advisability of a very large subsidy to this line if eventually we found that the cargo consisted largely of products or manufactures of the United States. Therefore we should have as definite information on that point as the hon. minister can give us.

My information is that but a small percentage of American goods is carried, except of the goods carried in cold storage,, of which there was a good deal carried at one time ; but I understand that now the Canadians are getting the bulk of that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: If these vessels are paid this subsidy for the purpose of carrying Canadian products, surely they should not be allowed to carry American goods.
I suppose the hon. gentleman would not refuse to carry American goods if there is room, and the shippers pay for carrying them ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Then it appears that we are subsidizing this line to enable American manufacturers to compete with ours.

No, on the contrary, supposing that these vessels carried 3,000 or 4,000 tons Canadian goods and were able also to carry 1,000 or 2,000 tons of American goods to fill up with, for which they would be paid, that would enable them to carry Canadian goods relatively cheaper.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: But the American government do not have to pay for that privilege.

If we have enough Canadian goods to fill the vessels, the Americans will send none. If there is a deficiency of Canadian goods, the vessels will take American goods. I do not think it would be very good policy to refuse the American goods when we have not enough of our own.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
That may be a matter of opinion. It is news to me that these vessels were permitted to carry American freight.
. The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE. I never knew of a case in which a clause was put in a contract forbidding the carrying of freight from any port, though preference might be given to Canadian freight.

We are paying $14(3,000 for this service to South Africa and it is
carrying American freight as well as our own.
It may carry some, but the great bulk is Canadian.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I do not know whether our boards of trade are aware of that fact.

I should say that if we desire to make the best of our routes, particularly the St. Lawrence route, so far from discouraging American goods going by the n, I should be glad to see millions of tons of American produce coming down the St. Lawrence and going in our steamships to other parts of the world. These goods will find itheir way across anyhow, and w*e may as well have the benefit of the trade.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Have Canadians got any better rates by reason of the space being filled up with American products than if American products were not taken ?

I think they would. If a vessel has accommodation for 5,000 tons and can only got 3,000 tons of Canadian freight, the chances are that the Canadian producer would get better rates if the other 2,000 tons were made up from any other quarter. You will have to pay this service what it costs to take the vessels from one side to the other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The only point is that we are subsidizing vessels to carry the products of a foreign competitor as well as our own.
The great bulk of the freight which we do send is our own, and I do not see that we will gain anything by prohibiting other goods.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman inform us what proportion of the freight is Canadian and what American '!
I doubt very much if ten per cent is American.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What is the average tonnage of these ships V

speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I understood that the American part of the cargo consists of goods that have gone in cold storage V
Some portion of it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: That would be food products ?
Yes, of course we ourselves are sending some by New York.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Where does this fruit come from ?
It is supplied us by the railway systems chiefly. Some come by the Grand Trunk Railway and some by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Where do we get our supply of American freight ?
The only trade we get is what comes across our lines of railway, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I understand that there are three companies, each getting a portion of this $146,000. Did any of the vessels call at Canadian ports before the government entered into this contract ?
Of course, the Allan Line did.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Did the others ?
Also the Elder-Dempster called at Canadian ports, but they did not go to South Africa.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Were any vessels put on after this contract was entered into 'i

New vessels were put on certainly by the Elder-Dempster Line. The Furness-Withy I am not sure of. The- Allan's have a large steamship fleet, and they relegated some of their vessels to this South African service. Several vessels formerly employed on other routes were put into the South African service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman any means of ascertaining what proportion of the cargo comes from the United States V

That is somewhat difficult, because we receive the goods from the railway companies and they do not discriminate between the two very carefully. We are obliged to approximate, but I think I am right in stating that the percentage is but. small.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I should like if possible to have definite information on that point.
I will try. It is somewhat difficult to get minute information. I can tell the hon. gentleman generally that the great bulk of the cargoes has been supplied by Canada.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Where did the hon. gentleman get that information ?
. The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE. From the steamship companies and customs.
Would it be unreasonable to inquire from the steamship companies what are the exact quantities that come from the United States '!

Certainly.
Steam communication during the season uf 1903. i.e.. from the opening to the closing of navigation, between Gaspe basin and Dalhousie or Campbellton, $12,500.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Is any ehauge being made in the service ?
This used to be performed by the steamer ' Admiral '. It is now being performed by a screw steamer of greater draught. But there has been some difficulty about getting into various harbours.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Has the contract been signed ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
I cannot allow this item to pass, Mr. Chairman, without thanking the Minister of Trade and Commerce for the trouble he has gone to during the last two or three years in trying to improve this service. I might also mention the right hon. the Prime Minister in this connection. The hon. member for Gas-p6 (Mr. Lemieux) and myself have been to see the right hon. gentlemen often in the last three years to try to get a more satisfactory service than has been given in the past. This service is from Dalhousie to Gasp6 Basin, a distance of 160 miles, along the whole county of Bonaventure and Gaspe. The county of Gaspe being entirely without railways, and Bonaventure the same for nearly one-third of the distance, great importance is attached to this steamship service. The old steamer ' Admiral ' performed this service for twenty-five or thirty years. But, though a good boat in her time, the ' Admiral ' is somewhat out of date. She was formerly the property of General Grant as far back as 1864. She is a paddle-wheel steamer, and, for that reason, not fitted for the route. For the last five or six years the people have insisted on a change and on a more modern steamer being provided. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce saw the reasonableness of the request and invited Mr. Connolly, who has the contract under the name of the North Atlantic Transportation Company, to secure a better and a more modern boat, and one propelled with a screw, so that she could start earlier in the spring and keep the service up later in the fall, for the service in the Baie des Cbaleur can easily be kept up for at least ten months in the year and a specially constructed vessel could ply along that coast for almost twelve months in the year. Paspebiac and other ports are open for the whole twelve months. Mr. Connolly

consented last year, at the request of the government, to remove the ' Admiral ' and replace her with a better boat. He went to England and secured a freight boat which he named the ' Restigouche.' This	boat has	been	performing the
service since the spring without a contract with the government. And I must say, the letters that	X receive from
my constituents are strongly to the effect that the ' Restigouche ' is altogether unsuitable for the service. She is a good freight boat, but not suitable for passenger service. And, in a country where there are no railways, the question of passenger accommodation on the steamboat is a very important one. There were very few cabins on the * Restigouche,' though a certain number have been added since she was put on this route. She is now performing the service in a more or less satisfactory manner without a contract; but, I presume that at the end of the season Mr. Connolly will come and ask the government to pay him for the number of trips he has made. There is published at Campbellton, New Brunswick, from which it is proposed to run this service, a newspaper called ' Events ', which is a non-political paper, and I believe, fair in these matters. It speaks of this steamer service, which, it should be remembered, is not only for the people of that locality, but for the large number of tourists who visit this section in summer. The editor of this paper went on one of the trips of the 'Restigouche,' and he has given his impression in an article of two columns and a half iii that newspaper. Of course, I have no intention of reading that article, but I may be allowed to read extracts in order to convince the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce of the necessity that exists for a change in this service. In a portion of his article the editor points out the requirements of a boat for that particular service :
What are the requirements for a boat for the Bay Chaleur ?
Not too commodious, but staunch.
Quick in getting under speed.
Very responsive to her wheel.
Not drawing a great deal of water.
Good speed out of port and prepared for a little ice in a late season.
The ' Restigouche ' is too long, while proportionately narrow, practically doesn't make a wharf at all, naturally slow in getting under speed, draws too much water, being a single screw boat Is helpless to back water, and except under speed her helm is not of service.
In short as to her present requirements she is out of her element
If she were here to make a through trip, Dal-housie to Gaspe for handling freight and accommodating passengers, with a little further care for those on board she would give good service, but that is not her work and far from it.
When the boat leaves Dalhousie at two o'clock in the morning, she has twenty-two or twenty-three stops to make before reaching Gaspe at ten or eleven o'clock at night. Being a coasting steamer, she is expected to go as near as possible to the shore. But a boat drawing sixteen feet of water cannot go near the shore and people have to go out in small boats and wait, it may be for twr or three hours, for the boat to come along One of the stops is New Carlisle ; but till first trip made by the ' Restigouche ' she passed by the shiretown of Bonaventure without stopping at all, to the great disappointment of the people. She had through freight for Gaspe Basin, and did not stop. The editor of ' Events ' describes her efforts to stop at Carleton, which is a well known summer resort. Where there is a splendid wharf with fourteen feet of water at high water :
Our first stop was Carleton, where in an effort to come to the wharf, it was sadly missed and the ' Restigouche ' found herself getting into the beach sand in her smugglings to keep to her element. Reversing her screw (and those who purported to know said that except when dead still it is not permissible at all) the whole boat shook from brow to stern, but she finally got back and a second effort brought her up angling broadside on the narrow end of the wharf. We need not here enumerate the sailors' efforts but suffice to say almost two hours were required to secure her to the posts.
It will easily be seen that a boat of that kind is not suitable for this service. What is required is a boat drawing not more than ten feet of water, or twelve feet at the outside ; a screw steamer that will break through the thin ice in Dalhousie and Gaspe Basin, in the month of April and keep up the service to the 1st of January. She should have proper passenger accommodation, and also be able to handle freight, because considerable freight is carried on that line. I have said these words in justice to my constituents, and I know that if the hon. member for Gaspe were in the House at the present time-he had to leave for Montreal this afternoon-he would have endorsed every word I say. I hope the right hon. minister will take steps which will result in an improved service next year. If calling for tenders publicly is the only protection we can have, I hope they will be called for early during the present season. It should be stipulated that this navigation should be kept up as long as possible, not merely at Dalhousie, because that is a landlocked basin where ice forms early in November, but be kept up for ten months in the year, where it can be easily kept up, in the Baie des Chaleurs. That is all I have to say. I once more thank the Minister of Trade and Commerce for the trouble he has gone to to secure us a good service, and I would ask him to excuse me for the trouble I have felt it my duty to put him to. The peculiar situation of these counties requires special attention to this steamship service.
The ' Restigouche ' has not given
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: This is done by a steamboat company to Campobello.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The only objection is that this vote is at least $1,000 less than what is needed to give the service we should have.

My hon. friend will find in the supplementary estimates something more for the purpose of carrying out that service.
Administration of the Chinese Administration Act. including remuneration to trade and com merce and customs officers, $5,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: There Is an increase.

We have had a good many more immigrants and a good deal more is received from them. The number of Chinese immigrants during the year has increased from 2,544 to 3,587 ; and the revenue has increased from $178,000 to $364,000. We are getting now about $500,000 out of the Chinese. I suppose when the present statute comes into force that will be stopped.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: By what means is the Immigration Act administered ?

Under the supervision of the controller of Chinese Immigration, but we chiefly employ customs officials and give them a certain allowance to look after these immigrants and to collect the poll-tax. The tax is chiefly collected at Vancouver or Victoria.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The amount received for the past year was how much ?
$364,000. For the present year the amount is estimated to be $526,000. One-half goes to us and one-half to the British Columbia government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What is the increased tax ?
That does not come into force till the 1st of January next. Of course the increased number is probablv due to anticipation on the part of these people.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
How many are in Canada at the present time, giving the number by provinces if it is convenient ?
The MINISTER OF TRADE! AND COMMERCE. I am afraid I will have to refer
the hon. gentleman to the census for the exact numbers. But about 20,000 are supposed to be in Canada now, the great bulk in British Columbia.
How many have come in since notice of the increased tax has been given ?

The number reported to have come in is 3,587.
Canada's proportion of expenditure In connection with International Customs Tariff Bureau, $600.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: This is a small charge that we pay to the customs bureau in Bruxelles.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What does it do ?

It is supposed to furnish us with information as to the changes occurring from time to time in the tariffs of the various countries in Europe and elsewhere. It is a bureau of information. We subscribe for the purpose of receiving early notice of the changes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Do we get an annual report ?
Yes, we get reports much more frequently than annually. We get the changes in the tariffs whenever any are made by the respective governments connected with this.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Are they published in the blue-books ?

Yes.
Commercial agencies, .improving expenses in connection with negotiation of treaties or in extension of commercial relations, $40,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: This is the same as heretofore. There have been four officers appointed since last year-one, Mr. Poindron, in Paris ; another, Mr. Jardine, in South Africa ; another, Mr. Ross, in Melbourne, Australia, and another, Mr. Ball, in Birmingham.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: How many commercial agencies have we altogether ?
Eleven.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: In what places are they established ?

There is Mr. Larke at Sydney, Mr. Ross at Melbourne, Mr. Jardine in South Africa, Mr. Ball at Birmingham, Mr. Poindron in Paris, Mr. Burke at Kingston, Jamaica, Mr. Bryson at Antigua, Mr. Hors-ford at St. Kitts, Mr. Tripp at Trinidad and Tobago, and Mr. Sontum at Christiana, Norway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman give us some idea as to the service to the country which these commercial agents render ?

The minor ones, as the hon. gentleman will see from the salaries fixed which are very small, report from time to time whenever they see any chance of trade and they keep us informed as to what trade is going on with Canada in their particular districts. The ones who receive larger salaries, such as Messrs. Larke, Ross, Jardine, Ball and Poindron, are expected to traverse the country more or less in which they reside, to report to us as a rule monthly, or oftener when required, and generally to advise us in what possible direction the trade of Canada can be developed. Of course, most of these gentlemen have been appointed very recently. Mr. Larke is the only old appointment. He has been in New South Wales for a considerable number of years.
speakername: The MINISTER. OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Have there been any new appointments during the present year ?
Yes, I gave them. Mr. Ross was appointed at Melbourne, Mr. Jardine at Cape Town, Mr. Ball at Birmingham and Mr. Poindron at Paris.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman give us his opinion as to the practical results which they get from this expenditure ? Does he regard this expenditure as well justified ?

Well, most of these gentlemen have just been appointed. Mr. Ross has only been appointed for six months, Mr. Jardine for about a year, Mr. Bail for two or three months, and Mr. Poindron for six or eight months. How far these gentlemen will succeed in developing trade and commerce I can hardly say as yet. They all appear to be very zealous in calling the attention of the communities in which they reside to the articles that Canada can produce and in making suggestions as far as they can to Canadian manufacturers and merchants as to what classes of articles are best adapted for the markets, in what way they should be prepared and generally how trade can be increased. I am in hopes that they will justify the expenditure of the sum which we are now asking for them, but in most cases the appointments are too recent to say how much or how little they may accomplish. Mr. Larke's reports which have been received for a period of six or seven years are very carefully prepared and I think he has done his utmost to promote trade with Australasia. This trade has shown a very considerable development within the last few years and I have no doubt Mr. Larke has contributed considerably to it. The other gentlemen, I think, will assist more or less in diffusing information, but it will rest, of course, very largely with the manufacturers and merchants themselves who may choose to take advantage of it. These officers discharge to a very great extent the functions which are discharged by the consular agents appointed by European countries under somewhat similar circumstances. You may regard them as Canadian consular agents.
Bounties on iron and steel and on the refining of lead. To cover expenditure in connection with the administration of the Acts, $5,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Most of this will be refunded by the parties to whom these bounties are granted. We are obliged, of course, to check the products and will be obliged to increase considerably our vigilance particularly in the case of lead bounties.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: There is an increasei of $2,500.
Yes, the hon. gentleman is aware that we are increasing the bounties on iron and steel and lead and probably there will he a considerable additional output in both of these cases.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I do not quite see, although the hon. gentleman seems to imagine I should, why an increase in the bounties would increase the expenditure.

It will increase the output and consequently will increase the amount of work that will have to be done, and moreover I suspect that the justification for giving the bounty is that a number of lead mines will come into operation which are practically idle now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: If it covers lead also. I admit there is force in the right hon. gentleman's observation.

It covers lead. We propose to make these parties pay the expense of inspecting them and seeing that they earn the bounty in conformity with the regulations.
Inspection of staples-chief inspectors, inspectors. deputy inspectors and other employees under the general inspection of the Manitoba Grain Acts, $48,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
These officers were in former times paid out of the Manitoba grain fund and they were paid by fees. We have deemed it better that these officers should receive a fixed salary, and that the fees should go into the consolidated revenue fund. We received from the fees collected up to June 30 of the present year $76,900, and the total expenses have been $65,000.

Inspection of binder twine, $2,500.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will the minister explain tvhy he appointed an inspector of hinder twine ?

Various complaints have been made to us by farmers and others that the binder twine was not up to the requirements, and we thought it expedient to make ' sure that the farmers' interests were duly protected, and we appointed an inspector at a salary of $1,200.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How can an inspector inspect a lot of binder twine ?
Probably in the same way as you would inspect barrels of apples, by taking samples and seeing that they correspond with the requirements of the law.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How will he do it-by taking samples ?

Each parcel of binder twine is supposed to contain a certain number of yards and, I think, a certain weight, and he can inspect a number of these parcels in the factories, and if he finds that on the average they are correct, he would be justified in assuming that the remainder are good. If he found there was a deficiency in any considerable number of these he would be justified in so reporting, and have the parties fined. There is a statute providing penalties in the event of binder twine being deficient in quantity or quality.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I do not think it applies to the quality, but only to the quantity. The statute provides that there must be a tag on each ball showing the number of feet per pound, and I apprehend that this inspector's duties would be to see that it contained the proper length.
He will see that the statute is complied with.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Will that apply to American twine as well as Canadian?
My instructions to him were to see that the American twine came up to the standard represented.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The importer is liable if the statute is not complied with.
Has the inspector been inspecting binder twine this season ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Has he reported to you ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Did he find any delinquents ?

He reported to me that as a rule the results have been satisfactory. I think they are allowed a deficiency of five percent, but if it is more than five per cent, they are liable to be fined. His report is that the majority of the manufacturers have complied with the law.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister might just as well admit that this was done for the purpose of giving a job to Mr. Joseph Haycock, who was the leading Patron element in helping the Liberals in the elections of 1806, and who deserved something at their hands. Mr. Haycock had to be provided for, and so they appointed him inspector of binder twine, something that there is no more use for than there is for appointing an inspector of mosquitoes. If he wants to inspect a ball of twine he has to unravel it, and that spoils the ball and the government will have to pay for it. That is about all Mr. Haycock has to do. The farmers of this country are shrewd and sharp enough to inspect their own twine when they are buying it.
It is just a job.
We would not do such a thing.
How did you manage to get along for several years without this inspector ?
Complaints were made to the department that the farmers' interests were neglected.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I suppose there is some correspondence with respect to this appointment ?
I don't think there is any correspondence.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: When was the statute passed providing for inspection of binder twine?
I am not quite certain, but it wras prior to the inspection being assigned to the Department of Trade and Commerce.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: And since it was passed the binder twine had been manufactured in the penitentinary without any inspection at all. Has there been any general complaint with respect to the quality of the twine manufactured ?
As to the penitentiary, I cannot say, but there have been complaints that the balls of twine were not up to the standard prescribed by the statute.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What are the inspector's duties ?

To go to the several factories at which twine is manufactured, and also to inspect from time to time the larger wholesale and retail establishments in which twine is sold. If he discovers any defalcation, he has to report and endeavour to have the party fined.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Seventy-five per cent of the twine now consumed in Canada is manufactured in the United States. Has the inspector anything to do with that twine ?
His instructions are to ascertain whether the twine sold conforms with the provisions of the statute.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: There was a time in the history of Canada when a large proportion of the twine consumed in Canada was manufactured in this country, but at the present time, since the free trade policy adopted by my hon. friend, 75 per cent of the twine used in Canada has been manufactured in the United States.
I am not prepared to say what the proportion is.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: That statement was made in the House, and I think it is within the mark. What I do not understand is that when there was a very large quantity of twine manufactured in Canada the government did not see fit to appoint an inspector, but now, when a much smaller quantity is manufactured, they think it necessary to have an inspector.

I do not think it makes much difference whether we have an inspector or not. The idea of appointing one man to inspect all the binder twine used in Canada is utterly ridiculous ; he cannot examine the thousandth part of it. I am inclined to think, with my hon. friend from Leeds, that the object has been a good deal more to find a position for Mr. Haycock than for any good he is likely to accomplish. I am sure that all the balls of binder twine lie will examine will not return very mufch profit to the farmers of this country. You would require to have fifty men, if you are going properly to inspect the binder twine used by the people of this country. Then, what is going to become of the twine that Mr. Haycock inspects ? A man cannot inspect a ball of twine without destroying it. Is the government going to pay the manufacturers or the agents whose twine is examined, for the loss they have sustained by reason of the inspection ? Because, when a ball of twine is once unwound, I rather think it will not accomplish the purpose for which it was made. I have heard it said that Mr. Haycock has some instrument by which he can rewind the twine, but I think he will not be able to do it in that scientific way required to make it run freely off the binder. There will be a considerable sum required to compensate the binder twine men for the twine lost in this way, and the minister had better put it in supplementary estimates.

What particular qualifications has Mr. Haycock for this position?
I did not think that a market gardener was specially qualified to inspect binder twine.
I presume that the reason Mr. Haycock got the appointment was because of the good he did the government in stumping the various counties for them. He stumped mine, but I do not think he did any harm, because he is too well known in that part of the country. I remember the Minister of Trade and Commerce once writing a letter in which he claimed that the Patron platform was the policy of the Liberal party, and economy was then a prominent plank in that Patron platform. I do not know what economy there is in appointing a man as inspector of binder twine because he posed at a Patron, .and at the same time stumped for the Liberals.
We would like the hon. minister to make a statement of the qualifications of Mr. Haycock for this appointment.
If the hon. gentleman has met Mr. Haycock, on the stump or anywhere, I think he will substantiate my statement that Mr. Haycock is a man of very decided intelligence.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: He has made a very bad use of it.
I have known men of intelligence in very high positions who have put their intelligence to a very bad use-not meaning anything personal to my hon. friend.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I did not understand that it was one of the necessary qualifications of a binder twine inspector that he should be a good stump speaker. I might remind the hon. minister that there is a very large number yet to be provided for. For myself, I wish to enter a protest against this expenditure, and I think I shall move to strike out the vote. As I understand the law respecting the manufacture of binder twine, it provides that each binder twine manufacturer must put a tag upon each ball, stating the number of feet per pound in the ball. If that is true, what is the necessity of having an inspector ?
Sometimes they make mistakes, and do not give the requisite number.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
This gentleman was appointed last June. There has been a very large amount of twine manufactured since then, and I suppose the officer has made some report to the department as to the duties he has performed-whether he has found that any of the twine manufacturers

in Canada Lave not been living up to the law, and whether the large quantity of binder twine imported into this country has been found to be up to the standard manufactured by the Canadian people.
He has made a report, and, so far as he can discover up to the present date, the twine manufactured corresponds with the regulations imposed by the law.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will the hon. minister bring down his report ?
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
If the hon. minister had appointed an inspector to see that the manufacturers did not make over 100 per cent profit, he might be of some value to the Canadian farmers. If the hon. gentleman will turn up ' Hansard ' of July 29, he will find that the Minister of Justice gave the prices that were paid for pure manilla each year since 1893, and if he will look at the report made by the late Minister of Justice, he will find that twine can be manufactured for f cents per pound. To that add the cost of the manilla, and a reasonable profit, and you will have the price at which the inspector should see that the twine is sold to the farmers. Double it, if you like, and you will see that the farmers have paid a good deal more. air. Clarke, of Toronto, asked :
What was the average price per pound paid each year since 1893 by the government of Canada for man-ilia used in the manufacture of binder twine at the Kingston penitentiary ?
The Minister of Justice stated in reply that in 1893 there was none purchased: In 1894 the price was $4.38 per cwt. Add 75 cents for manufacturing, and you have 5 cents per pound. In 1894 twine was sold to the farmers for about 6i cents. In 1895 the cost of manilla was $4.13; in 1890. $4.46; in 1897, $4.26. In 1897 the farmers of Canada paid about 13 cents a pound for binder twine. This thing has been going on under the eyes of the government for several years, and why did they not appoint an inspector before to see that the farmers were not being overcharged ? In 1898 it cost $3.71 for pure manilla according to the Minister of Justice. Adding 75 cents for the cost of manufacturing, that would give $4.50 per hundred pounds, yet the farmers paid 13 cents in 1898. In 1899 pure manilla cost $3.39. In 1900 none was produced. We purchased enough in 1899 at $5.39 to do for another year, yet in 1900 it was sold away up from 12 cents to 15 cents. And this government put the blame on the war for the heavy prices they were charging. In 1901 it cost $7.54, and in 1902, $6 per hundred pounds. Adding 75 cents for the manufacturing. that would make $6.75, and giving a cent per pound profit, you have $7.15. Yet, it was sold from 12 to 13 cents. In the

face of these facts, why do the government not see that the farmers are not obliged to pay two or three times the cost of vhe production of twine. There was something for an inspector to investigate. The government have appointed Mr. Haycock, market gardener, at a salary of $100 per month and travelling expenses, which will amount to another $100 per month, going around the country to see that the manufacturers put a tag on each ball, showing the correct measure. Surely the hon. minister will allow this item to drop and pension off Mr. Haycock, or give him some other work to do.

The right hon. the leader of the House pleaded yesterday that he was carrying out a moral obligation. Let me draw his attention to this fact. We are told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that Mr. Haycock has superior qualities and was very eloquent on the stump. We also know the right hon. gentleman once sent a letter to this institution, of which Mr. Haycock was one of the prominent members, endorsing its policy. What policy had the Patrons at that time ? Criticising the extravagance of the government. I remember very well the hon. gentleman, when he was on this side, raising his hand to heaven and denouncing the extravagance of the Tory party in spending $35,000,000 to govern 5,000,000 people. I call upon the right hon. gentleman to carry out now the pledge he made while in opposition to reduce the expenditure of the government $3,000,000 or $4,000,000. Does he think he will reduce it by employing this man at $1,200 per year? The right hon. gentleman must feel very sad when he thinks that this government are not carrying out the principles they advocated in opposition.
I do not think that at all.

Circumstances alter cases. The hon. gentleman has a very satisfactory berth and is willing to throw to the winds all the promises he ever made. All his anxiety is to retain office. I challenge him and the Minister of Trade and Commerce to point to one principle which they advocated on this side that they have not thrown to the winds. They excuse their extravagance in every instance by the plea : 'Oh. we have inherited this from previous governments.' Well, they did not inherit this particular item. What has become of the $60,000,000 which they have frittered away ? They have not inaugurated one scheme which they ever intended to carry out. They have now before the country a scheme which I do not believe they intend to carry out. The only ambition they have is to keep in office as long as they can.

One of the highest tributes paid to the present government is every allusion to the fact that the patron in-

dustry-an organization that grew into great strength and influence because of the extravagance and iniquity of our hon. friends opposite-has disappeared since the present government came into power.

AIN, We should have some explanation as to the qualifications of the gentleman appointed to this position. When you appoint an inspector at a salary of $1,200 and expenses, or equal to $2,500 per year, we naturally expect him to have some qualifications for the position. I would like to ask the hon. minister whether there has been any complaints made to the department that the twine manufactured and imported into this country in years past was not up to the standard, and if the Patrons of Industry or the farmers have made any general demand for the appointment of such an officer.

There have been complaints that the quantities provided by the statute were not furnished to the farmer. As regards the inspector, I think that a gentleman of his intelligence and general ability is quite able to discharge the important and onerous duties assigned to him.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman say that this officer is really required in the interests of the farmers V

I think it desirable that the farmer should be protected. We should see that he is supplied with the quantity of twine, which the law provides should be contained in each separate spool. It will be found that the farmers of Canada, who are not over and above well regarded in the distribution of patronage, approve as a rule of the appointment of one of their number to see that the provisions of the statutes are carried out for their benefit. Moreover, I have heard from several parties that they were glad to find the government had taken action.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman present those letters to the House V
I am afraid that many of them are marked confidential.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: It is rather a reflection on the Minister of Justice that the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce should employ a man to watch over the government output, and see whether the twine turned out has a tag giving its length. I wonder if the hon. minister has got a report from the manufacturer at Kingston. For it is quite possible, if others put up twine at short length, that it may be done there. But it seems that the government have to appoint farmers to watch their own operations.
My hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) thinks we need a good deal of watching, and has said so a good many times.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
I hope that no reflection is being cast upon the patrons or the farmers, because I was a patron myself. I was elected by the patrons to keep down the expenditure of the government, if I possibly could. They elected me to see that justice was done to every man, if I knew what justice was, and they thought I did. There is just one point I wish to emphasize, and that is this, the manufacturers and the importers of binder twine, knowing that there is an inspector of binder twine will be very careful to make the ball full length. There is that point in favour of the appointment of an inspector of binder twine. The question is whether the right man has been appointed, and whether the appointee should be a gardener, a farmer or something else. I am in favour of farmers for every thing. I think a farmer could be found to be the First Minister for that matter, and more particularly Minister of Trade and Commerce. However, I do not want to make this a matter of guess, but, I want to say that the money paid to the inspector will be well earned if all the manufacturers and importers of binder twine are compelled to see to it that there are 650 feet of binder twine to every pound. I met the inspector of binder twine a few days ago, and he told me he had visited a large number of manufacturers, and watched tlieir operations, and lie found some of them were ' sailing very close to the wind ' whatever that means. That was his language, and I infer that he meant that they were hardly giving the farmers justice. I said-and put emphasis on what I said- ' Now, Sir, your reputation is at stake ; and if you find any man not doing his duty and not giving us fair measure, bring him to justice.' He said he would. I am not one of those who cavil and think the office of binder twine inspector is a useless one. If the inspector does his * duty fairly, his salary will be well earned, and I hope the minister will see to it that the inspector does his duty. .

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I have not the slightest objection, but I say it should not be done as a matter of course, and without calling the attention of the House to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We will do it in future.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

House again in Committee of Supply.
Inspection of binder twine, $2,500.
['The resolution stands on the Notice paper, and its formal stage will be taken on Monday.']
When the committee rose at six o'clock the h'on. minister was to give us a report oS the inspector.
The deputy informs me that he is not in a position to produce the information to-night. There is no formal report, though there are some letters from the inspector.

I understand that the binder twine factories are scattered all over Canada. For instance, there is one in Brandon, Man. Does the minister think it is possible for one man to inspect all the binder twine in this country, if it is necessary to have it inspected at all ? If it is necessary, would it not be better to have an inspector paid a small salary and located in each town or city where there is a manufacturing establishment, so that the inspection would be an inspection in fact as well as in appointment ? The inspector should be there when the factory is in operation, which isi only a short period in the whole twelve months.
No, the manufacture of binder twine goes on for a very considerable time throughout the whole year.

There are a great many months in the year when the binder twine factories are not in operation at all. I think my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Heyd) will bear me out in that statement. The factory in Brandon is not in operation more than six months out of the twelve. I repeat, if the department has decided that it is necessary to have an inspection, would it not be better to appoint a man where the factory is and have the twine properly Inspected ?

The Minister of Trade and Commerce thought that as a beginning one officer might do a large amount of inspection. I fancy that the value of an appointment of this character is not so much for the cure of the evil as for the prevention of the evil. The hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) stated this afternoon that the knowledge that there was such an officer, who might come in and inspect at any moment, would have an excellent effect on any manufacturer or dealer. If we adopted the policy suggested by the hon. member for Peel, it would not only involve the appointment of an inspector for each factory, but one in each town where there is a dealer. It may be that the method of inspection is not as broad ns it should be. We shall have to learn by experience how far it may be necessary to extend it.
Has the binder twine imported into this country to have the same number of feet to the pound as that manufactured in Canada ?
Yes, the regulation applies to the imported article as well as the manufactured article.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Where is the great bulk of the twine imported into Canada manufactured ?	[DOT]
I cannot tell the hon. gentleman. Probably 'lie is aware himself.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am. The hon. Minister of Justice knows that we have on the statute-books a law prohibiting the importation into Canada of any article made in the prisons of the United States, and I believe that from one-half to two-thirds of the binder twine imported into Canada is manufactured at the Stillwater prison, and Is sold to agents at the big binder twine establishments in Minneapolis and St. Paul, and by them exported to Canada.
Have you any evidence to that effect ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have information to that effect which I believe to be true.
Convince us by giving us the information.

If my hon. friend has that information in a form that permits it to be used, he as a friend and protector of the manufacturers of Canada has been doing them a great injustice in keeping it to himself, because he is well aware that if he placed that information at the disposal of the Minister of Justice every pound of that binder twine would be prohibited from coming into Canada at all. I am afraid my hon. friend is not as good a protectionist as he professes to be.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I came into possession of the information within the last six hours,
and as soon as I received it I addressed the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Justice, whose duty it is to see that the law is enforced. If the hou. gentleman inquires, he will find that there is a large quantity of binder twine made in the Stillwater prison, and if he traces that product, lie will find that a great proportion of it is landed in Canada.

But my hon. friend, in justice to himself, should not be content with a mere statement in parliament. That statement is of course entitled to respect, but after all it is not a basis for action. If he has that information. I think he should place it in possession of the Minister of Customs in such a way as to enable him to follow it up.

What is this army of inspectors for ? What is the armv of customs officials for if not to attend to cases of this kind ? Why play the bluff game of asking my hon. friend from Leeds to inform the Minister of Customs. What is this army of heelers appointed for except to trace the binder twine that is imported and find out where it was made ?
I am sorry that the hon. member for Victoria characterizes the customs officials as an army of heelers.
Now it is time to drop a tear.
It Is time to drop a tear ; but the hon. gentleman cannot refer to an army of inspectors of binder twine, because there is only one, though of course sometimes one is a host in himself.

Is that all ? I thought there were several. I apologize ; I thought there was an army, and that this last one was the chief of the outfit. I trust that the minister will see that this new officer attends to his duty and traces this prison-made binder twine, wherever it comes from, and sees that it does not come into Canada.

It seems a curious thing that the binder twine makers have sent deputations down here and told the government the difficulties under which they laboured, and yet not a single representative of the binder twine makers ever made that statement to the government : and to assert that the International Harvester Company and the Plymouth Company, who sell 90 percent of the twine sold in the United States, would be guilty of palming off on their customers either on this side or on the other side prison-made twine, is something that the hon. gentleman himself does not believe. If the statement which the hon. gentleman now makes is true, the men who make the binder twine would be aware of it and would have brought it to the attention of the government long ago.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is not the twine made in the prison as good as that made in the factory outside? Do they not turn out as good binder twine in the prison at Kingston as in the city of Brantford ? In the United States the prison manufacture is probably the best twine turned out in that country. Where is it sold ? It must compete with the other twine manufactured in the United States, and I am informed that the whole outfit of the American prison goes into the hands of gentlemen who supply the trade in Canada.
The trade in Canada is supplied by the International and Plymouth people.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They do not make it all.

They make 90 per cent of all that is used in the United States and send 16,000,000 pounds to Canada. It is not likely that a concern of that importance would sully its reputation by palming off prison-made twine, even if it were as good as that made in the factory, which it is not. No factory in Canada would palm off prison-made twine for its own.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: All I ask the hon. Minister of Customs to do is to put a detective to work and investigate and he will find my statement correct.

I would not like to say that all the officials in the Customs Department are heelers, but there is one thing I am sure about, and that is that the gentleman who is receiving this appointment is a political heeler. He has been active from place to place in every byelection held in recent years.
What do you mean by heeler ?

A man who seems to make his living by stumping in constituencies and doing such work as his party requires. This gentleman spent nearly a month in North Grey during my by-election, and now he is apparently receiving his reward. I must say that I do not think he was any particular advantage to the Liberal party, but rather a source of strength to the Conservative party, and I would like our hon. friends opposite to send out that class of heelers at every election. Why should he receive a government appointment worth $2,500 ?

The vote is for the inspection of binder twine, $2,500. If he does not receive it in salary, he will receive it in some other way. Here is a man who is nothing but a political heeler and has been so for years, then he is placed in charge of certain government work, while officials who have been in the service for years are pressing the government to pay them $000 or $700, and are unable to do so. What are this man's duties ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: To draw bis salary ?
