My hon. colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, fully explained that this afternoon. Was my hon. friend present ?
Perhaps both could not tell the same story.

That is a good reason why I should not tell any.
I understood my hon. colleague to have explained that the object was to guarantee to the farmers that each of these parcels of binder twine contains the quantity it should contain.

How is he to make this inspection? There is a tag on each ball giving the contents, so many feet to the pound. Do you mean to tell me that this inspector is going to measure each of these balls of twine ?
Not all of them.
He will, I presume, go into a factory and measure one ball and certify that it is 650 feet long. If he does not measure it, how will he inspect it ?
He will weigh it.*

These packages may weigh two or three pounds each and may be measured and stamped. It seems to me that this is another case of providing for friends of the government for whom they can find no other place.
What are the special qualifications of this official ? He may be a politician and not have qualifications for the office to which he has been appointed.

I was fortunate enough to be present ten minutes before recess and heard my hon. colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, say that this man was very intelligent and capable of doing the work assigned him, and he thought the farmers would be pleased to have one of their own appointed to this position.

One would suppose that the gentleman appointed to an office of this kind would be an expert, should know how to discern what is sisal and what manilla, of what is the substance the binder twine is composed of. It may be a simple thing to take a ball of seven yards of twine and ascertain by weighing how much is in the ball. Anybody could qualify to do that in half an hour's experience. But to understand what the substances are that the binder twine is made of would require a man of considerable experience. The committee would like to know the qualifications of this man ?
He is not a manufacturer of twine.

I see the hon. Minister of Justice there. It appears to me that the manufacture of binder twine, as carried on in the Kingston penitentiary, has not been satisfactory to the people. The price of twine during recent years has been very high, and the farmers have complained very much. I notice by the Auditor General's Report that twine which the Minister of Justice said cost 6 cents per pound, was sold to the farmers at 104 cents. That would appear an unreasonable profit. Twine imported into the country, made of pure manilla, is sold at from 10 to 15 cents a pound, but this is a mixed manilla. If it only costs 6 cents per pound, why is the farmer charged 10J cents ? When the farmers refused to pay that price, it remained on his hands, and later in the season he could sell it at 5J cents to some of the government jobbers.

It is very good of the hon. gentleman to give me an opportunity of explaining the discrepancy. It would be convenient for me, indeed, if the hon. gentleman would attend when the estimates are under consideration. If he will kindly refer to ' Hansard,' I have not the number of the page under my hand, but I will be able to find it and give it to him-he will learn all the details. I gave all the details of cost of twine and the reason why we were hot able to dispose of the twine during the season required and had to keep it over. He will get the information and more if he will kindly refer to the ' Hansard ' report of the debate which took place when he did not happen to be in the House.

I have the Auditor General's Report for 1902, and I find that at page M-47 it is noted that the government sold 6,783 pounds of mixed manilla, at 10J cents per pound. And the hon. minister stated early in the session that it cost 6 cents per pound.
I do not accept the statement of the hon. gentleman.
I will look it up in ' Hansard.'
If the hon. gentleman will do so, he will then be in a position to give some information to the House.

Then, the department sold 10,000 pounds at 101 cents, and 220,000 pounds at 5 1-10 cents, or less than half the money. It would seem to me that the farmer is being imposed upon. This institution was established in the Central Prison to regulate the price, so that the farmer might not be imposed upon by any combination in this country or any other. The local government established 244
a similar institution in the Central prison, for the same purpose. And, as my hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd) is here, I may say that the Farmers' Binder Twine Company was established for the same purpose, yet, that hon. gentleman has stated in his place that that concern made no less than 240 per cent in three years, besides being able to make great improvements in their plant. The Kingston penitentiary was making twine for 6 cents per pound and charging the farmer 10J cents per pound, the same prices that were being charged by American firms selling the goods here. There seems to have been some understanding among the manufacturers to charge the farmer more than is fair, for-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the committee is wandering away from the point under discussion. We are not discussing the general question of the manufacture of binder twine, but the propriety of appointing an inspector to see to the proper measurement of the twine. I hope the members of the committee will not enter upon irrelevant discussion.
The only reason I adverted to this question was that the Minister of Justice was not present when-this was brought up.
The hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Thomson), was not present.
How do you know V
I was here.
Well, I was not lecturing in the Young Men's Christian Association anyway.
I am afraid there is no danger of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Thomson, Grey) having any opportunity to do that.

The Minister of Justice was not in his place, and the Minister of Finance took note of that and apologized for his colleague's absence. But, if we are not allowed to discuss the question of manufacture, there is still a good deal to say as regards the appointment of this inspector, and I must say that I will support a resolution to strike out this amount. It is simply making an office for a party heeler. The service can be performed for much less money than the allowance given to Mr. Haycock. If other appointments under the government are made in the same way as this, it is no wonder that the expenditure of this country rises to such an enormous sum.

I could understand if such an appointment could be useful at all, that it might be made useful by the appointment of some man who had had experience in handling or manufacturing binder twine. But Mr. Haycock's qualifications are of an altogether different char-

acter. This is simply the creation of an office for the benefit of Mr. Haycock. He has qualifications, but they are rather of a kind that are useful in a by-election. But nothing I have ever heard or read about him would lead me to believe that he has any qualification for this office. The name might suggest a knowledge of grasses, and so, of cordage of some kinds, but there is nothing in a name in this case. This office is useless to anybody but Mr. Haycock himself, and the money paid to him could be devoted to some useful pui'pose.
When was the Act passed making it necessary for the manufacturer to put a tag upon each ball giving the number of yards per pound ? Can the hon. minister read us that clause V
I cannot point to the particular Act, it was passed some years ago.

If that is all the law provides, what is the use of this inspector ? If the law only requires that the tag shall be put upon the binder twine, why should this inspector be saddled upon the people ? What are his duties ?
I do not think the farmer is so desperately anxious to know that the tag is on, but what he wants to know is that the quantity corresponds with the tag.
Then, all that this inspector will do is to test one ball. And for this you employ him for the whole year at $2,500 of public money.

In any case where inspection takes place, I imagine every package is not inspected. When a number of parcels are sent through the customs house the officers do not inspect every one, but they sample them. I sui>
pose the same will be done by this inspector.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: As I understand the Act, it makes no provision for an inspector. It simply provides that every manufacturer shall put a tag upon his products stating the number of feet in each ball. In that case, every farmer can be his own inspector; and if he finds that the twine does not meet the requirements of the law he can set the law in motion to have the penalty enforced. When he buys a ball of twine that weighs what the Act calls for and has the number of feet in it required by the law, the farmer can be his own inspector, and there is no need of paying $2,500 in salary and expenses to Mr. Haycock to make the inspection, because he has no more effect on the production of binder twine than if he remained at home attending to his market gardening. The last time I met Mr. Haycock was at a provincial election where he was speaking in the interest of the Reform candidate

against my friend Mr. Gallagher, who was the candidate for Frontenac in the local election. I was speaking on behalf of my friendi Mr. Gallagher, and I drew attention to the fact that the last time I met Mr. Haycock was at a Dominion by-election, when he had the Auditor General's Report in one hand and a can of Australian mutton in the other, pointing out to the farmers the iniquities of the late Conservative government, and showing by the Auditor General's Report that they had bought so many jack knives, so many envelopes, so many sponges, and a lot of little things like that, reading them out of the Auditor General's Report and then holding up the can of mutton.

That shows he can read.
Mr. TAYLOR Oh, yes. He served his time iu the provincial legislature, and was appointed leader of the Patron party that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Postmaster General created. They created this Patron party for the purpose of helping their elections and splitting up the Conservative party. Mr. Currie was another leader. Mr. Currie is appointed immigra-tiou agent now over in the United States, drawing another $2,500 a year. I would suggest to the minister that Mr. Currie be authorized to go over and see if the binder twine that is being imported into Canada is not made in prisons. They wanted to give him a job. There is a third one. Mr. Lockie Wilson, that they have not provided for yet. He is the third gentleman who was a leader of the great Patron party. Two of them are provided for at a large salary and they have nothing to do. My hon. friend can turn up the Auditor General's Report and find that Mr. Currie, who was a leader of the Patron party in the west, is now in the employ of the government over in the United States, riding around in Pullman cars at great expense to the country, and drawing a big salary besides. Mr. Haycock is provided for at a salary of $1,200, and $1,300 for travelling expenses and hotel bills, for the balance of the year. My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Heyd) who is interested in the binder twine establishment up there, knows that every word that I am saying is correct, and that there is no more necessity for an inspector of binder twine than there is for a dozen inspectors, one for each factory.

I am afraid our friends are not so hostile to the position of au inspector as they are to the gentleman who happens to fill it. I just wondered to myself whether if Mr. Haycock had been busying himself in the interest of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) and his friend Mr. Gallagher, we would have heard one word of objection to the creation of this office.
We have heard it from you.

I do not think so. The mere fact that the office happens to be filled by Mr. Haycock is the reason why all this objection has been urged. Had it been filled by a good, active Conservative organizer we would not have heard a whimper from the other side. '

It really does appear from this discussion that this is an entirely unnecessary office. Any farmer going into a store to buy twine and looking at the tag and seeing how many feet to the pound are stated to be in the ball, can demonstrate that to his own satisfaction and can prove it to the dealer at once. It will not take him more than a minute to do it. He can take a few yards and then weigh it and find out at once whether it comes up to the standard which is stated by the tag upon the ball. Anybody is qualified to do that. The only other object of the inspection of binder twine is to find out whether it contains the right proportion of manilla and sisal. If it makes no provision for that, then the office is entirely useless. If Mr. Haycock must have a positiofi, I would suggest, after hearing [DOT] the discussion the other night in regard to the killing of chickens, that probably Mr. Haycock understands this business, and the government could give him a job of going around and teaching the farmers how to kill chickens.

I think the minister should give the committee the Act under which this gentleman is appointed. There was a special Inspection Act for binder twine, passed either in the session of 1901 or 1902. I would have thought that if the government intended to appoint an inspector, some provision would have been made for it in the Act. I do not think the acting minister would say that there has been any demand from any section of the farmers or of the merchants selling binder twine, for an inspector to be appointed. I am quite sure the office is an unnecessary one. I think, under the law, there is a penalty for the Infringement of its provisions. This looks to me like an after-thought on the part of the government. The gentleman no doubt was pressing for some appointment, and this position seems to have been created for him. I am not opposed to the inspection of binder twine, but I think if it is to be inspected some better system should be adopted. I am sure it is impossible for one gentleman to inspect all the binder twine that is produced and imported into this country. The minister must be aware that a large quantity of binder twine is imported into western Canada and the province of Manitoba. There is some manufactured in Manitoba, but a very large quantity is imported.

The argument of some lion, gentlemen opposite is to the effect that because there is a certain law passed that does not require an inspector to be ap-24U
pointed, therefore no inspector is required. We have on the statute-book at the present time a law requiring that weights and measures should be of a certain standard size. According to their argument now no inspector is required to see that that law is enforced. I suggest that they turn then-guns for the time being on the gentleman who happens to occupy the position of inspector of weights and measures for western Ontario, who happens to be a good Conservative, retained in his office by the present administration. Now, if their argument is of any force that because there is a law on the statute-book requiring weights and measures to be of a certain standard size, they do not require to be inspected, and therefore they would do away with the services of that inspector, as they are proposing to do away with the services of Mr. Haycock ; by the same process of reasoning, all the license inspectors should be dismissed-I know in their opinion they should be anyhow. But it is illegal to sell liquor after certain hours, it is illegal to-day to do certain things in connection with the hotel business.
It is necessary that an inspector shall be appointed to see that the Act is enforced and I think the same thing holds good in reference to the appointment of an inspector of binder twine. I do not think it comes with very good grace particularly from our hon. friends opposite to make use of the arguments which they do against the appointment of Mr. Haycock. What is Mr. Haycock's offence in their eyes ?-simply that he has taken an active part in political campaigning. He has gone out and done stumping-to use a common phrase-in different parts of the country. If that is a serious offence, then, our Conservative friends themselves have a great many heelers among their numbers, because I know there were some of them in the riding of the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Thomson). I think their argument is a very weak one and that it comes with bad grace from a party who, while in power, were continually appointing persons who had been political heelers to various offices within the gift of the government. I think the fact that a man has a certain amount of ability qualifying him to take part in a political campaign should not stand in the way' of his getting political preferment. Besides that, Mr. Haycock, whatever his offences may have been, is a practical farmer. He may have been the representative of the Patron party, as he was no doubt, but he is a practical farmer, he knows a great deal about the binder twine question, and I think the people generally would approve of his appointment and endorse the government for having placed him in that position.
Was Mr. Haycock appointed chief inspector or an inspector as mentioned here ?

The deputy minister will be here in a moment and I will be able to give the hon. gentleman an answer. As far as I know there is only one inspector, but whether he is designated chief or otherwise at the moment I cannot answer.
Generally when the term ' chief inspector ' is used there are deputies under him, but in this case it would appear that there is only the inspector himself.
I have 'no doubt that is so. As the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Ross, Victoria) says he is an inspector and I would therefore ask the hon. Minister of Finance for what division he has been appointed ?
I am sorry I cannot give the hon. gentleman the information.
I suppose we must ask that of the deputy ?

There was a pretty full discussion of this item before recess and I thought the right lion. Minister of Trade and Commerce had satisfied the laudable desire of every hon. gentleman opposite for information, and that all I would have to do would be to call the item and it would be carried at once. I am amazed that it should not pass.
I am amazed that the hon. gentleman does not know more about it.
I do not pretend to know very much about it.

In looking at the statute I find that the government, when appointing an inspector, are required to designate the" district for which he aets. When a chief inspector is appointed he is appointed for the whole province, it is true, but when a division superintendent, who is called ordinarily an inspector, is appointed, he is appointed, apparently under the statute as follows :
The Governor in Council may from time to time, designate the several cities, ceunties, towns and other places or inspection divisions in Canada, at and for which respectively it is expedient to appoint inspectors.
I presume that the hon. Minister of Fin-anc, looking over this matter, has considered whether Mr. Haycock should be an inspector of a particular division or not and if he is appointed simply as an ordinary inspector for a division, a particular county or a number of counties, or for a particular city, or district, the fact should be designated by the Order in Council. I think we are entitled to the information, because, as far as I see there is about as much foundation for the appointment of this particular inspector as an inspector of binder twine as Mr. BARKER.
if he were appointed as an inspector of haycocks.
It is surely reasonable to ask what division he is going to act in 1
The whole includes different parts.

No, the statute clearly says that there shall be an inspector for a particular district and a chief inspector over the inspectors. I would like to know whether Mr. Haycock is an inspector of inspectors or an inspector of binder twine.

The statute may enable us to appoint a great many inspectors, and an inspector of inspectors, but as an economical and businesslike government we do not deem it necessary to make any more appointments than the public interest demands. If it is found that Mr. Haycock can cover all the ground then it will not be necessary to put the country to the expense of a second appointment.
Is he the only one ?
He is the only one up to date. He has only been appointed within two months.
You do not know but that you will want more.

It is coming on towards harvest time. Mr. Haycock is a man highly respected by the class who use binder twine. For many years he enjoyed the confidence of the- farming community as representing their views upon public matters. I have no doubt he still enjoys that confidence and he is particularly qualified in so far as a knowledge of the farming community goes to guard their interests in a matter of this kind. However, as hon. gentlemen opposite are complaining we have not appointed enough we will bear that in mind, and if, after the harvest season has gone by, experience shows that the appointment has been productive of good and if we are satisfied that the public interest calls for an additional appointment we will have to do our duty, but do not blame us because we have not rushed in and appointed a whole army of officers at once. I believe an hon. gentleman earlier in the discussion called one an army. We have not gone that far yet.
The hon. Minister of Finance explained that he is a whole host in himself.
No doubt he is a very capable man.
The explanation of the hon. Postmaster General shows that he has not read the Act.
Yes, I have.

The Act empowers the Governor General in Council to appoint inspectors for certain divisions and presumably the Governor General in Council .will authorize the appointment of inspectors where they may be necessary. To-day there may be an inspector required in Brantford. Possibly such an inspector was very much required when the manufactory there was making 240 per cent profit on its business. It would have been a very proper thing for the Governor General in Council to appoint an inspector for that district and for different places where it might have been found necessary to appoint inspectors. But, the government when they had appointed half a dozen or more Haycocks, or inspectors throughout the country might have found iti necessary to appoint a general inspector to overlook the whole of these, and that is provided for, but the hon. gentlemen have begun with a general inspector and if he should be the only one that begins the work then he should be placed where his inspection is required to be done. If the hon. Postmaster General had read the Act he would have seen that the whole spirit of the Act was that the government should begin at the districts where the inspection is "required and after they had provided for a number of districts they ought to have appointed a general inspector. The very term implies that he is an inspector of inspectors. They have begun with a general inspector who has one general district of inspection.
Would the hon. minister tell us what are the duties of this inspector and whether his instructions are in writing ? It is not unfair to ask that we should have a copy of that.
I am informed that when he was appointed he received instructions, but I did not imagine the question would be asked. I shall be glad at a later stage to produce this valuable information.
It is very important, because I understood from the Postmaster General that this is only the first of a series of similar appointments.

There is no such inference to be drawn from my remarks. We propose to appoint one inspector, and if it is found that one is not sufficient for the work, we intend to appoint more, but gentlemen opposite are endeavouring to drive us into making a large number of appointments. We are a government of economy; that is one of our strong cards ; we enjoy the confidence of the country because of that, and we intend to stand by that principle. The only thing that will drive us from it will be a due regard to the public interest, and if the public interest demands two inspectors, we will appoint them. The hon. gentleman from Hamilton desires us to put on frills before
we have the fabric and to appoint an inspector of inspectors. What we are doing now is the appointing of an inspector of binder twine.
The Act says you must designate a district.

The
Act says :
The Governor in Council may from time to time designate the several cities, counties, towns and other
Hear, hear, that is the whole contention.

The
hon. gentleman has a habit of interrupting when something is being said or read. If he will have the kindness not to interrupt me until I read two lines he can interrupt at the end of the third line:
The Governor in Council may from time to time designate the several cities, counties, towns and other places or inspection divisions in Canada.
The statute does not say we ' must ' do it. This Act was passed by our opponents, and does the hon. gentleman say that it was intended to force the government to divide the country into districts and appoint inspectors That has not been done in a single case.
Then it is all wrong.
Does the hon. gentleman from Hamilton say that all Canada is to be divided into inspection districts for every article mentioned in the statute ?

The only authority to appoint an inspector is under this Act, and the Act says that until you designate districts you cannot appoint inspectors. Let me ask the minister whether a board of examiners has certified that this gentleman is a fit and proper person to conduct this inspection. The Act requires that he should obtain a certificate from a board of examiners of certain boards of trade. Has that been obtained ?

Let us stick to one point at a time. This Act has been in force since 1896, and I am informed by the deputy minister that in no instance has such an interpretation been placed upon the Act as the hon. gentleman now puts on it. There is only one case in which there is a district set apart for inspection and that is in the case of grain. This Act deals with the inspection of flour, meal, wheat, beef, pork, leather, fish oil, hides, &c., and by the Act of 1901, binder twine is added to the list. Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker), say that all the appointments. since this Act became law are illegal ?
I did not say that.
Then he argues that they are illegal when made by the Liberals but not illegal when made by the Conservatives.

The Act requires that your inspector should get a certificate from a certain board of examiners.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL Have you abandoned your other argument ?
No.
Either that or you are defeated.

Not at all. Under this statute the first step of the government is to name a district in which the inspector is required, and the next step is to obtain a certificate from a proper authority that the person to be appointed is competent to fulfil his duties. Even this very government required a board of trade of which I was president to send certificates that certain persons were competent when they were to be appointed as inspectors.

This matter is one of great seriousness. I listened to the scientific part of the debate with great pleasure, but now there is a nice legal question lying at the bottom of the appointments that are to be made. I undertake to say that it is a local jurisdiction that has been created by this statute, and it is elementary law that a local jurisdiction must be definite and distinct before an officer can exercise any authority under that jurisdiction. My hon. friend is a lawyer. Let him take the case of a justice of the peace who is appointed for a city or county. He cannot act for one moment until the territory for which he is appointed is defined. If he did, every act he performed would be without autho-irty, and he would be liable for an action. The point my learned friend has made is quite clear. The Act says that ' such inspector shall hold office during pleasure, and shall act within such local limits as the Governor in Council assigns to him.' How does my hon. friend, who, I understand, is a lawyer, in name at any rate, get over such plain and distinct language 1 My learned friend takes a very illogical position in arguing that as the government were only going to appoint one inspector, there was no necessity of assigning local limits. If you only wanted to appoint one inspector for the province of Ontario, the proper course would have been to pass your Order in Council declaring the province of Ontario to be one district. If you want to appoint a man for a county or a city, you must first plot out your county or city, and declare that that is the territory and these are the local limits in which you desise the inspector to act; and then he would have jurisdiction to act within those limits. This inspector can be kicked out of every store in Ontario ; and you do not want the gov-Mr. BARKER.
eminent to send unauthorized men to act as inspectors and to run the risk of being put out. If such a man were put out, the Minister of Labour would be put out at the same time, because his agent is the minister himself in law: and how sorry I would feel if any indignity were put upon the Minister of Labour. A gentleman of his commanding stature ought not disrespectfully to be put out of any place in this country. But if he persists in acting in the face of the law so plainly pointed out by my hon. friend from Hamilton, who is no doubt a very careful lawyer, he has only himself to blame. But the next difficulty my hon. friend pointed out was that you have two classes of men to appoint. You have the familiar illustration of the stipendiary magistrate and the justice of the peace. You must define in your commission whether you want to appoint a stipendiary magistrate or a justice of the peace. They are officers with different jurisdictions, and you must first define your territory and then appoint your officer. So in this case you must state the jurisdiction you expect your officer to exercise, whether that of local inspector or inspector in chief. These are such elementary principles in law that I thought the hon. gentleman would have caught on at once, and would have said : ' My duties as Minister of Labour have so occupied my attention that I have completely overlooked this particular matter.' I should have thought he would have thanked the astute counsel from Hamilton for having suggested so plain a matter to him. The next point raised by the hon. member for Hamilton was that you cannot appoint a sub-officer unless you have a chief. However, I will not debate that. There may be such a thing as appointing an inferior officer without appointing a superior. It would seem an extraordinary thing to appoint a chief without a sub, and equally extraordinary to appoint a sub without a chief. Ex necessitate the hon. gentleman appears to be wrong. But even if he got past all these difficulties, there is the certificate. I can understand that this law was very wisely framed. It anticipated the hon. gentlemen opposite coming into office at some time, and therefore it should be provided that this man should be examined as to his competency before he should be appointed. On these three points, I have no doubt that the hon. minister as a lawyer will say at once, ' peccavi.'
I do not think you can pass this item, because it is contrary to law.
We will take chances.
We will not allow you. We do not want you to get into a law suit.

It is a serious matter if it was our duty to appoint an army of inspectors', and we have neglected to do so; but for the present our

sense of economy would not permit us to appoint more tlian one. There is a great deal to be said for the bon. gentleman's argument that we are obliged to appoint a large number of inspectors; but do not ask us to commit ourselves to such a policy too early.
That is not the point of my argument. You could not appoint anybody under the present state of the law.
That shows how the opposition are not consistent with one another. The hon. member for Hamilton says we cannot only appoint an inspector, but an inspector of inspectors, and keep on appointing them.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me? I said you can appoint an inspector and a chief inspector, provided you follow the provisions of the Act, and I say that you have not followed the provisions of the Act.
The hon. member for Colchester says we cannot appoint anybody.
Not until you plot the territory.

Well, suppose we do plot the territory and appoint a large army ?
' Mr. GOURLEY. But you cannot appoint anybody until you plot the territory.
We will take that into consideration. We may make further appointments, but we do not think it is necessary at present. I do not like to throw down a valuable suggestion like that.

Does the hon. gentleman seriously tell us that there has been any certificate from the body required to give a certificate under this statute? Does he tell us that this gentleman who is to be appointed is a proper person to be appointed under the statute ? Under the statute the government have no right to make such an appointment at all, and we object to it on that ground.

Surely there must be some satisfactory answer given to the statement of the hon. member for Hamilton, if he has stated the law correctly. M e assume a certain amount of responsibility for this appointment, and we want to know the fact.

I think we may regard the matter in a broader view thap has been suggested here. I have not seen the appointment, nor do I know what principles have been observed in regard to it. The requirements of the statute may have been complied with or they may not, but the appointment itself could be made if there were no statute, the only question would be what powers the inspector would have. He cannot discharge any
duty unless authorized to do so. But if in a general and informal way the government appoints this man to discharge certain duties and the twine manufacturer permits him to exercise those duties, and if that meets the requirements of the case, why put the country to the expense of the appointment of a large number.
That would not follow.

Yes it would. You could not have a large number of inspectors without putting the' country to a great expense. Suppose there were no statute at all and the government appointed a man to do certain work and parliament voted the money to pay him, and the manufacturers permitted him to inspect, the same end is obtained as by going to the expensive process urged upon us. If the law is that no inspector can be appointed for more than a limited territory and this whole Dominion is to be divided up into inspectorates, involving very large expenditure, it seems to me that the Act ought to be amended and made more in harmony with economy.

The way to amend an Aet of parliament is not by a resolution in the estimates. The Act of parliament requires a certain procedure before such an inspector as the one now proposed, may be appointed. The hon. gentleman says that the government may appoint certain officers; but when an Act of parliament intervenes, declaring how an officer is to be appointed, it does not rest with the government to appoint him in some other way. I do not think any hon. gentleman on the government benches would controvert that position. This is not a question of giving Mr. Haycock or any other gentleman a government allowance. This is a question of inspecting a certain matter of trade in this country. There are a number of articles that have to be inspected. There is the article of hides. It is very important that the inspector of hides should be competent, and it is impossible to get a man appointed inspector unless he undergoes a certain examination and obtains a certificate from a particular body that he is competent. Hon. gentlemen know that upon the certificates of such officers trade goes on throughout the Dominion. The certificate of an inspector such as the one to be appointed, is accepted in all the markets of the country. The inspector of hides at Hamilton gives certificates, which are accepted at Montreal, Quebec and Boston, as those of a person qualified for the work. People all over the United States and Canada deal to the extent of thousands of dollars upon that certificate. If the government can appoint Mr. Haycock without a certificate of competency, they might also appoint in the same way an inspector of hides and wheat and other articles, and thus disturb the trade of the whole country. The

statute provides that the inspector must have a certificate and we object to any resolution authorizing payment to any person who is not appointed according to the statute.

There will be great *difficulty in connection with this man. He will have important duties to perform, and if properly appointed his authority would be effective and valid, but if not, he will be simply a trespasser and be liable to be sued for trespass, and every body who sent him would be responsible. If not properly appointed, he could not act as an officer of Canada, he would be a pseudo officer, and have no authority at all. If it be the case that the stamp of our inspector of hides is received in Boston or in Montreal as official, is it not most important that the appointments of other inspectors should be perfectly regular ? What a scandal would it not be to allow a man to give an official character and market value to a hide and then have his appointment declared null and void. If the department has not observed the statute strictly, it is time it should do so. When an officer is properly appointed his district is prescribed and just as in the case of a judge. Imagine a judge being appointed and the territory of his jurisdiction not defined. The limits of this man's jurisdiction must be as strictly defined as those in which a judge exercises jurisdiction. If this man's territory be not defined, he can exercise no jurisdiction, and if his territory be defined he can only act within that territory, and any act outside it would be void and the department be responsible. We want to know whether this man's commission defines the territory in which he must act. The second point which my hon. friend from Hamilton made is that a deputy inspector shall be appointed only from among duly qualified persons. There may be, therefore, but very few people who may be appointed. The appointment is subject to extraordinary limitations. It is limited to very few political heelers, if men of that class are not wholly excluded.
I think a man who could get an appointment under this statute would not be likely to be much of a political heeler. Perhaps he might be a divinity student, or a Ph. D., or an LL. D. This Act confines the appointment to ' qualified ' persons. What that qualification is, I am at a loss to understand. And perhaps this should be submitted to the Supreme Court to get a judicial interpretation of the statute. The minister must understand it. I can only regard it with the eye of the student of language, and so regarding it I say that mountains of difficulty; difficulties alpine in their character surround the minister or the legal adviser of the department In connection with this question. Talk about standing on thin ice. Why, there is no ice here at all. A man would be in the water up to his neck

when he attempts to make an appointment under this statute. It provides that ' they and their deputy inspectors shall be appointed only from among duly qualified persons.' I cannot understand what qualifications they must have. I would like to ask what qualifications the minister found in this man ? Were they scientific ? Were they religious ? Or literary ?
Some say they were political.

That would not do under the Act. I can see that my hon. friend, being much interested in politics, might think that this statute referred to political qualifications. But if he considers it as a student of literature, I think he will see that that is an error. I am sure, from the speeches the hon. gentleman has made in this House that his mind is illuminated with the classics, English, Greek and Latin. If a man's mind is so illuminated, he acquires the quality of realizing the importance of words. Why, a word appears as big as the side of a house to him. He notices differences that to others would be imperceptible. He is struck at once with an accusative, or a dative, or an ablative absolute. The student of words taking up this statute would be struck at once with this peculiar phrase, ' and they and their deputy inspector shall be appointed only from among duly qualified persons.' If I were in office and it were my duty to make an appointment under this statute, I would naturally touch one of these numerous beds that seem to ring all over the department and bring numerous officials to the minister's side. I would call one of these men, perhaps a literary man or a doctor of laws, and I would say to him, ' tell me what ' qualified ' means in this statute. If he were a student of statutes and accustomed to construing them, he would at once see that these words do not relate necessarily to scientific qualifications, in short they are not words of nomenclature, therefore, they must be defined in the Act. Then I would look through the Act for a definition of ' duly qualified persons.' But looking through the Act I do not see any such interpretation. I am driven then to the conclusion that the words must receive the ordinary interpretation of these words in the English language. What, then, does duly qualified mean ? It may refer to a person who has been immersed-in that case he would be duly qualified to enter the Baptist Church, or if it meant duly qualified to enter the Church of England, it would require that he should be able to pass an examination in the thirty-nine articles. Of course, if he belonged to the church of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser), he would have to be able to recite the shorter catechism word for word and letter for letter.
Yes, and lie would know that lie must give an account of time; therefore, he would not kill time.

And he must also he familiar with that stately confession of faith called the Westminster confession. But since that hon. gentleman (Mr. Eraser) has entered parliament, they are doing away with the confession of faith. I suppose that as the hon. gentleman has been so long supporting the government they find it necessary to modify it in order to retain him; for one could hardly support this government for such a length of time and be ready to accept the old confession. But 1 am making a strictly legal and technical argument, and the hon. gentleman ought to understand that I am approaching the question scientifically and as a lawyer. Can the hon. learned gentleman help me to find out what is a duly qualified person under this Act 7 For, he will observe, if any other person is appointed, that appointment is illegal, and I am satisfied that the government would not wish to appoint a person illegally. I never saw a case beset with so many difficulties, and yet the minister seems never to have had one of them called to his attention. I venture to say that every one of the appointments made under the Act is irregular and void under this statute; and if the writs were sent to the Minister of Justice, that hon. gentleman would advise : You have not a shadow of a defence ; read the statute; and reconstruct your department. I would like the Minister of Justice to tell me what these words mean. He may say that this Act was passed under a Tory administration. If that is his answer, I can only say that the Tory administration had a poor draftsman. And, as to that, 1 think the draftsmen employed by this parliament are not good. You find singular provisions of the law clothed in different language. We ought to have an English draftsman, no matter what we pay him, so that when we wish to make a certain provision, it shall be clothed in the same language, every comma in its place. Then, when a section is judicially construed, it helps in the construction of every other. But in our [DOT]country different language is used to express the same idea, or, if the words are not varied, they are used in varied connections. I am amazed at the difficulties one finds in turning over these papers. The Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir William Mulock) could never have read this Act, could never have considered these difficulties. I can understand why all these provisions were necessary.
You were appointing an officer with extraordinary power. For instance, you could put up the Minister of Labour. As for the Minister of Finance, I think he did it more as an ad captandum reply to our friends on this side, because he is a shrewd Nova Scotian, and he catches on quickly to a
way of avoiding difficulties. But the Minister of Labour has seen fit not to reply, even by way of warding off attack. I have no doubt he intended to appoint more than one chief inspector, and perhaps one deputy. But I would not urge the second point. If he appoints one chief inspector in, the province of Ontario, he must name the province. He can name the whole territory of Ontario if he likes. He can say that for the purpose of chapter 99 the whole province of Ontario shall be one inspectorial district. Then he could proceed to find out what a properly qualified person was, and having found that out, he could, from among these people, select one of them. You cannot say that ' qualified person ' has no meaning, you have got to find a meaning for this phrase, and every word of that section must be read in, connection with every other word. The human mind is supposed to be capable of interpreting fully even a statute of the legislature. Some statutes, I admit, are very difficult to construe, because they are often not drawn with much care. But the judge who interprets these will say. I do not know' whether these men in the! House of Commons knew what they were doing or not. but for myself I am bound to give this language the most reasonable interpretation I can. I am bound to assume that they did know what they were doing. A judge is bound to find a meaning for these words ' qualified person,' otherwise he will hold this officer to be improperly appointed. It is no excuse for my hon. friend to say that he appointed Mr. Haycock. He might as well have appointed a cock of hay, and attempt to justify it under this section. I think my hon. friend was illogical in another respect. He said that Mr. Haycock covered the whole field. Why, in Nova Scotia we have dozens of haycocks and they do not cover a field. So my hon. friend has not a nice sense of language. I think a minister of the Crown should select every word he uses with the nicest care, with the same care that the Roman senators used when speaking. Once a barbarian came from a distant province that had been conquered by Rome, and hearing one of the senators pronounce a speech, he returned to his barbarian home and told the people to submit at once to the power of Rome, because, he said, the senators were gods and spoke as gods. Now how could any uncouth, unlettered person come into this House of Commons, and, looking down upon the grave and reverend seigneur, the Minister of Labour, and hearing him. in his most inartistic manner, discuss this statute, how could he return and make to the people of his distant province such a remark as that which was made concerning the Roman senators ? Surely the people of Canada should require of their ministers language as precise as that of the Roman senator.
I am bound to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that Rome never ruled over as much territory

r79<j
as the parliament of Canada rules over today. At the proudest moment of Rome's power she never ruled over 3,000,000 square miles ; whereas the hon. gentleman, by the extraordinary1 conduct of fate, is permitted to rule over 3,750,000 square miles of territory. Now I desire in the interest of Canada that the Minister of Labour, for whom I have the kindliest feelings, and whose fine ability I am bound to say-that is, I assume that he has a fine ability, because X assume that any gentleman who becomes a minister of the Crown has fine ability, although he may successfully conceal it from the public for a long time. But to-night I am going to assume on behalf of the cabinet of Canada-for I am bound to respect that body-I am going to assume, no matter how violent the assumption-we are commanded by law often to make violent assumptions- I am bound to assume that the Minister of Labour possesses that luminous mind that would enable him at once, when his attention is called to this statute, to give us all the benefit of a clear and distinct explanation. If he lias it not at hand, he will send and get us the original records of his department in which these appointments were all pointed out, and show us, before he asks us to pass that estimate, that every condition precedent to a legal appointment has been made.
To cover law costs and other expenses connected with deferred payments of bounties on iron and steel, $3,879.39.

This item arises out of the fact that there was a difference of opinion between the department and the Auditor General with respect to the claim of the steel companies for the payment of bounties. The question at issue was whether pig-iron, in the molten state, should be considered to be pig-iron, whether it must first be allowed to pass into the form of solid pig, or whether it was technically pig-iron as it came out in a molten condition. The department took the view, under the best information it could obtain, that the parties producing this iron had a right to claim the bounty upon it in the condition in which the claim was presented. There had been changes in the method of producing pig-iron. Formerly pig-iron was cast into solid pigs and passed in that stage into the next process for the manufacture of steel, but with the advancing methods of manufacture, that process was abandoned. The Auditor General took the ground that inasmuch as this pig-iron, in passing into the next stage of steel, was not cast into solid pigs, therefore it was not pig-iron. The matter was discussed for some considerable time, legal opinions were taken upon it and finally it was decided to have the case determined by the Exchequer Court. The decision was in favour of the company and against the view taken uy the Auditor General. Thereupon the bounties that were claimed were paid Mr. GOURLEY.
but in the course of this transaction legal expenses were incurred in trying the case and it is to pay these legal expenses that this vote is asked.

I remember when the bounty on iron came up discussing this particular phase of the question. There was a bounty on pig-iron and a bounty on steel. I asked the government at that time if the company did not convert it into pig-iron and then into steel they would get the bounty for pig-iron and also for steel. The answer, if I remember correctly, at that time was that they would get the bounty for pig-iron and also for steel. I also drew the attention of the government to the fact that in the modern method of manufacturing steel it did not go into the form of pig-iron at all, but that it was converted at once into steel, and I asked the question at the time whether they got the bounty for pig-iron as well as for steel. I do not recall the exact terms of the answer given, but it seems to me that it was that they would get bounties on both iron and steel.
That is possibly correct.

Why did the government not appeal ? I do not wish to reflect in any way upon the judgment of Mr. Justice Burbidge, but in a matter involving so much money I would have thought that the government would have appealed, because 1 know there has been a great deal of speculation at the bar in regard to whether the judgment was scientifically or legally sound. I am bound to assume, in deference to the judge who pronounced the judgment, that it was, but I was surprised that the government did not think it wise to appeal, so that the question would be settled by a full bench. As a matter of fact, the judgment of a single judge does not settle anything. Any lawyer has a right to differ from him. but we are bound to bow to the judgment of the full court.

Apart from the question of law, there was a question of equity in it. Suppose that it should be assumed for the moment that the judgment of the court was wrong, the company might have proceeded to convert this pig-iron into solid form for 24 hours, and then to have passed it on to the next stage. It would simply have imposed a little more labour and a little more expense upon them, and I do not know that we have any object in forcing them to go to unnecessary trouble of that kind.
Would it not have lessened the bounty that the government had to pay?

No. it would not have lessened the bounty, but it might have made it a little more expen-

sive fcSr tlie company in tlie method of production, by obliging the company to go through the process in the old way rather than in the new. It would have made no difference in the amount of the bounty.
Does the hon. minister remember what we are paying in iron bounties now?
I understood that it made a considerable difference in the bounty. If it did not, I do not see why the company were so anxious to contest that suit.

They found the modern method cheaper, and of course we might have forced them to adopt the old cooling process that had hitherto been followed, but it would have made it cost a little more in the production.
If that is the only point, I agree with the view of the hon. gentleman.

In the manufacture of steel by the modern method it is just as cheap to manufacture steel as pig-iron. You can bring out pig-iron in the same process as you can bring out steel, and the cost of manufacturing one is very little more, if any more, than the cost of manufacturing the other.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why these law costs when we have a Solicitor General's department to look after these matters ? Why should we have paid these outside lawyers when we have the hon. Minister of Justice and the hon. Solicitor General? When hon. gentlemen opposite were on this side of the House they took that ground.

We in the' Department of Justice advised the Auditor General to the best of our ability. He refused to accept the opinion we gave and took outside advice. After he took the advice, we thought it better to allow the case to go to the court, as the advice he obtained differed from the advice we had given. The matter having been referred to the court, the result was that the opinion of the Department of Justice was sustained in its entirety.
What were the costs?
There were experts brought from all over the United States to testify.
That includes witness fees ?
Yes, some of these experts were paid as high as $150 a day.
Does that include solicitors' and experts' fees.

Yes, the whole business.
Inspection of Staples-Expenditure in oon-nection with inspection of grain and flour under the General Inspection and Manitoba Grain Acts-Governor General's warrant, $16,000.
How was it that you required a Governor General's warrant?

That was a case where the appropriation was found to be insufficient, and it was necessary to have an additional sum. As we had no provision to meet this expenditure, we had to obtain a Governor General's warrant. This service is self-sustaining. We have to vote the cost in the ordinary way, but the fees fully pay the expense.
What is the total amount required for inspection?
$50,000 with the present vote.
What were the fees?
Will the hon. minister excuse me for asking one more questim about the bounty on steel? What was the Auditor General's objection if there was practically no difference in the amount of the bounty?
I suppose the Auditor General felt that it was his duty to give the treasury the benefit of all doubts, and having a doubt in his mind he took legal advice.
If there was no difference in the payments that were to be made whether it was molten or solid, what doubt or difficulty could exist in the Auditor General's mind?
If the court had sustained the contention of the Auditor General, the company could not have collected the bounty on iron at all.

He said that being in liquid form, notwithstanding that the ingredients were absolutely the same, it was not pig-iron. In order to be pig-iron, he held that it was necessary that it should go through the cooling process.

With such astute officers, I think the revenue is safe.
Culling timber, $17,500.
What is this for ?
This is the usual vote, with some very slight change.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is the revenue from this ?
About half of the cost is refunded by the revenue.

This expenditure, I think, is one that the timber trade ought to bear itself. This is for the purpose of paying cullers of timber down in Quebec and probably other places. The fees received for the culling used to pay the expenses and leave a surplus, but now there is a deficit.
We used to have twenty-eight cullers on the list, and twenty-two of these have been superannuated, which accounts for the increase in the superannuation allowance.
There is no necessity at all for six cullers in Quebec ; no timber goes there.
Oh, yes.
Very little.
Who are these gentlemen?
All good old Tories. They have been in the service for a very long time.
Notwithstanding that the trade is decreasing, the cost of the clerical staff has increased from $5,950 to $6,100.
Are they Tories ?

Every one of them. I do not think we need trouble very much about the salaries there, because the larger part of the amount is for the salary of the supervisor, Mr. Paton, who has been there a very great number of years, and for whose salary we may be providing for the last time. He is a very old man, and I am sorry to say that he is not likely to have another salary voted to him.
I suppose you find it almost impossible to dismiss civil servants or reduce their number in Quebec.
We are very partial to the old men we have there.

In connection with the items for the Trade and Commerce Department, I would like to call the attention of the acting minister to a question which was brought to the attention of the department last year. It has reference to the list of articles which are mentioned as entitled to preferential entry into the markets of France. Salmon is not mentioned on that list, but there was a shipment from our province accepted last year, while there was another shipment which they refused to accept. I would like to know if the deputy minister can inform the minister as to the condition in which that matter stands at present.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The MINISTER OF FINANCE, The deputy minister informs me that the French government have not consented to take our view of the matter. They still adhere to their interpretation of the tariff as respects that item.

There must be some misunderstanding about it, because one shipment that had been refused entry was afterwards accepted under the preferential tariff. The shipper himself informed me of that, and through me there was some correspondence on his behalf with the department.
Was it by direct shipment ?

It was by a shipment which was accepted as direct. As you are aware, we cannot ship direct in a ship sailing to France from our province, because there are none, and the shipment would have to go by rail to some of the eastern ports. There have been several shipments made, some of which have been entered under the preferential tariff. My object in bringing the matter to the attention of the department is to point out that while fish is mentioned on the list, canned salmon is not mentioned, and the French authorities claim it is not entitled to preferential entry. I wish to know if the department has taken any steps to have salmon placed on the list; lobsters and other fish are on it.

My recollection of the treaty is that it reads : ! Fish in its natural form,' or something like that. I do not think it specifically mentions the kind of fish, but I would not be sure about that. The main difficulty we have is the question of direct or indirect importation. If goods are sent by way of an English port and thence to France they do not treat that as a direct importation. If goods are sent by New York, strange to say, in the case of one line which seems to be recognized to some extent by the French government, the French Atlantic line, the French government have been willing to recognize goods carried by that line as a direct shipment. I am informed that the department has presented the matter to the French authorities, but so far without success.
The shipment I refer to was made in the same way as lobsters and other fish are sent.
Was it -made from a Canadian port ?
It was made from New York, by a French vessel.
They do admit lobsters sent by the French line under the treaty.
If you look at the schedule you will see that it specifies the fish by name.
Perhaps it does.
At the time the schedule was arranged there was no shipment of salmon in view, and it is likely an oversight on that account.

I will call the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to it, and, of course, we are all anxious that the salmon of British Columbia should receive the benefit of the minimum tariff if we can get it.
Very well.

I wish to call the attention of the committee to the supplementary estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals for the past year, in part I have been able to bring down the information which the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) asked for, and the rest I will bring down at a later stage. I would be very glad that as far as possible hon. gentlemen opposite would facilitate the passage of these estimates, reserving to them' selves the right to discuss similar items in the main estimates, which are yet to come, for the reason that the year has passed and gone and the accounts have to be closed up. It is of the utmost importance that these accounts should be promptly closed or otherwise the Auditor General cannot do his work, and the consequence would mean delay at the beginning of next year, I trust that hon. gentlemen opposite may be able to let the present estimates pass with as little discussion as possible, but, of course, I would not expect them to waive their right of inquiry or criticism.
Murray Harbour branch and Hillsborough bridge, Prince Edward Island Railway, $450,000.
The hon. minister was to bring down some information with respect to the Prince Edward Island Railway.

The hon. gentleman asked me to divide the item of $300,000 and show how much of it was for each branch of the service. It is as follows : For the bridge, $155,156.43 ; for the branch, $87,567.98 ; for fails, $45,000 ; for ties, $7.300 ; for rolling stock, $1,375.60 ; for land, $5,600. These items aggregate in round numbers $300,000.
What is the amount expended during the year under each head ?

For the year 1902-3 the expenditure was :	On the
bridge, $404,257.62 ; on the branch. $329,220.86 ; on the rolling stock, $9,515.52.
The hon. minister promised to bring down information as to what the rolling stock was.

Under the contract dated July 2, 1900, the contractor is to have the free use of two locomotives and twenty-five cars for ballasting, track laying, surfacing and trimming. He has had these since last summer. They are not new locomotives or new cars, but the smaller ones which have been in use for some years. He applied for additional locomotives and ears in May, 1903. Two locomotives and fifteen cars have been hired to him at $5 a day for each locomotive and 30 cents a day for each car. He has therefore a total of four locomotives and forty cars.
These supplementary locomotives and cars are not those to which he is entitled under the contract ?

No. He is hiring those at a price.
Hon. Mi-. HAGGART. What possible object has the government in furnishing capital to this contractor, for which j.t receives an interest which is totally inadequate 1
Of course, under the contract he was to be allowed the use of these. The consequence was that his tender was lower than it would have been if he had to furnish them for himself.

The minister does not understand me. I am not referring to those to which he was entitled under the contract, but to those which were furnished to him subsequently at so much a day. Why do you furnish him.with something that he is not entitled to under the contract ?
The road is approaching completion, and we shall require this rolling stock for the road. We could not afford to wait for it until the last moment.

It will be entirely useless when the road is finished. Is it sufficient justification to say that the rolling stock may be valuable after the road is completed, for purchasing rolling stock long before it is required for the road, and leasing it or giving it to the contractor ?
The road can be finished probably this autumn down to Murray river, and we would not have the rolling stock on hand for any great length of time.

No matter whether the road is finished or not. the minister must see that a wrong principle underlies this action.
Prince Edward Island Railway-to provide and lay steel rails, $13,400.
Is this the total amount that has been expended for steel rails during the past year ?
Yes.
What are these rails used for-for the purposes of the contractor solely ?
These are not for the Murray Harbour road. They are for the main line of the Prince Edward Island Railway.
What weight of rails are these ?

The last time the estimate was up, there was some negotiation with the United States regarding the erection of this darn. What is the total amount expended V
The- MINISTER OF FINANCE. The matter is making very satisfactory progress with the United States but is not yet settled.
Are you making the dam without their consent ?
This is not for the dam, and the dam should not be included.
What amount has been expended and what was the original estimate for that channel ?
The estimated total of that work when completed is $1,354,410.42, including the dam.
What was the amount estimated before the work began V
The original estimate for 200 feet was $750,000. The width was afterwards increased to 300 feet. My deputy cannot remember the estimate made under the amended plan.
Will this $80,000 complete it V
There is a further appropriation of $18,000 asked in the main estimates. These two items will complete it.

$1,302,000 for a work entirely useless and not required at all for the navigation of the river.
Galops canal-enlargement, $25,000.

As this item will create a long discussion and, the hon. member from that district is not here, I would ask to have it stand over. I would ask also that the next item, $25,000 for depening and widening Galops rapids be allowed to stand over as there will be a vote for the purpose of striking it out and a full discussion.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. member for Grenville informed me that he wanted this to stand as the money asked for has not been spent.
My information is that the work was done some time ago.

There never was work done for the payments made there.
Items allowed to stand.
Welland canal-to lower mitre sills of lock two and guard gates, $9,000.
I move to strike out that item.
I would like to know if the mitre sill is a foot higher than the navigation '!

Yes, there was a mistake made some years ago in the engineering.
lion. Mr. HAGGART. Exactly the statement I made a couple of years ago when the item was under discussion, and I was informed that there was no mistake whatever.

Motion agreed to.
Welland canal-to remove obstructions and make other improvements, $30,000.
This is for deepening portions of the long level. The contractors have made better progress than anticipated, and a further sum of $30,000 is required to close the work to the 1st July.
What, for tilling in the long level ?
For removing obstructions and taking out centre piers.
That is an enormous sum for taking out piers, there must be something else.

There ore $95,000 in the main estimates. This is not only for the removal of piers but also for the putting in of new spans. The channel was found too narrow and those piers had to be removed.
Mr. LANCASTER, At what part of the canal are these ?
It is known as the Long Level. I do not know whether my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) can identify it by that.
That stretches over many miles. At what part of the Long Level is it ? If the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) were here, he could tell us.

I remember the hon. member for Welland urged

It as of great importance to tlie navigation of the district.
I suppose it is in the town in which the hon. member (Mr. [DOT]German) resides.
I cannot give the name of the precise spot.
There is only one spat where it can be.
It is between Fort Colborne and Welland, but the deputy cannot tell me the precise spot.
It is between one extremity of the canal and the other. The hon. gentleman's (Hon. Mr. Fielding), information is precise and to the point.
If my hon. friend is acquainted with the-

I know where it is exactly. Better pass on to the next.
Welland canal-land damages, Grand river, 3625;
Surely the land damages are done on the Grand river. This is of no use to the navigation of the Welland [DOT]canal, and the sooner it is abandoned the better.
This is because of damages to land by flooding [DOT]caused by the construction of the Duunville dam.
Why, this dam was erected forty years ago, and there are land damages every year. Who are the parties ?
One of the claimants is W. T. Anthony, $500 ; Phillip Dufford, $97.27.
He must have .been kicking a good deal ?
Was that the way in the old days ?
That is the way now.
The Department of Indian Affairs had two claims of $14.63 and $13. I do not suppose that department has been kicking very much.

The sooner the government is relieved of responsibility in reference to this branch of the canal, the better. It is of no use to navigation, and has been abandoned since the Lake Erie level was adopted. The Grand river in connection with the Welland canal is a totally useless work.

And, so long as it is there, there will be land damages to pay, if the government is willing to pay them. Every [DOT]one knows that this is a district of low
level, and is bound to flood in some part every year.
Laehine canal-electrical appliances for operating lock gates, bridges and weirs, $20,000.
What is the total amount of this improvement ?

This is to provide power house, flume, necessary machinery, power for work shops, Ac. The expenditure up to 30th June, 1903, was $67,895 ; and the amount required to complete the work is $30,000, making a total estimated cost of over $97,000. I cannot explain why the appropriation asked is only for $20,000, making $87,000. However, that is an error on the right side.
Were these works only commenced last year ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is the work being done under contract ?
Yes. There is one contract of $12,925, with Mr. Pringle, for electrical apparatus, and there are other items making up the total to over $19,000 out of the $20,000 we asked for.
Was the rest of the work done by contract ?
Yes, the principle part of it.
What part was not done by contract ? One would think that all these electrical appliances would be supplied under contract.
All the electrical appliances, I am advised, were procured under contract. But there were a number of services and other supplies that could not be contracted for.
The total expenditure", including this vote have been $87,000. But what amount of that is done by contract ?
I was confining myself to an explanation with regard to this vote of $20,000, I cannot give the facts with regard to the previous expenditure, but I will get that information and bring it down.

I think I ought to move to strike out this vote entirely. We often hear complaints made of tu'penny ha'penny expenditures on the harbours of Nova Scotia, and it grieves me to see millions of money thrown into these canals in Ontario.

This is for Quebec.
Mr. GOURLEY'. But it is necessary to and tributary to Ontario. I find that these canals have been squandering money for half a century to develop the trade of To-

ronto. Now, I am not sectional. I never uttered a sectional word in my life, and I hope I will be spared the necessity of doing so. But when I hear hon. gentlemen from Ontario begrudging, apparently, little trifles that we need for harbours and steamers in Nova Scotia, I am shocked when I see these extraordinary sums voted with such carelessness for Ontario. I think there must be an end of these enormous expenditures on these canals, unless there is some compensation given in some way to the maritime provinces. We are tired of these eternal expenditures upon Ontario. We in the maritime provinces are tired of being the milch cow of this Dominion. As some compensation last year I readily agreed to the knocking off of the tolls on this canal, because anything that would benefit the trade of Ontario benefits me. I represent Ontario as much as any of these gentlemen here. Yes, under the law of this country the Minister of Justice would tell you that I represent every foot of Ontario as well as my own county. Now I want the freight rates on the Intercolonial lowered as a compensation for doing away with the tolls on the canals. I cannot see why this Bachine canal should be free, why we should vote this enormous sum of money, $20,000, to make bright and beautiful this canal for these gentlemen from Ontario who sail through it in their pleasure yachts. The item reads ' Electrical appliances for operating the lock gates, bridges and weirs.' These gentlemen travelling down from the wealthy cities of Ontario cannot wait, apparently, to have these locks opened in the ordinary way ; this country must furnish them with the most modern electrical appliances for that purpose. 1 suppose when the Minister of Customs desires to go on one of these pleasure trips down the St. Lawrence he cannot be bothered with having these opened in the ordinary way. That is all right, he wants to lead the strenuous life, I suppose. But at the same time I want to make the po'int that we must have some compensation for this extraordinary expenditure of money on these canals. We are getting tired of it in Nova Scotia, and we are not going to put up with it any longer. Therefore I think these gentlemen from Ontario should agree to cut the rates on the Intercolonial 50 per cent.
Make them free. .

The people of Ontario are not generous enough for that. We would be satisfied with a cut of 50 per cent. Or else I will move to strike out this item for lighting luxuriously the locks on the Lacliine canal. It is the most extraordinary thing I ever heard of-electrical appliances for operating lock gates ! I am told this is the latest and most modern thing in the history of canals. The people of Ontario are never satisfied with anything. They expect us in the maritime provinces to Mr. GOURLEY.
be satisfied with any old thing that happens to come along. We have been satisfied long enough, and now we want more railways. The province of Nova Scotia is practically without railways. If it had not been for the kindness of Providence in throwing the ocean around us, we would have been barbarians for the want of communication. But the sea has given us means of communication by which we have been enabled to keep in touch with each other, and keep our language and civilization in a measure intact.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask the hon. gentleman to confine himself to the question.

I move to strike that item out. I ask the Minister of Finance whether he is prepared, in compensation for these enormous votes that we are called upon to pay in the maritime provinces, to make us some compensation in the way of reducing rates on the Intercolonial.

I want my hon. friend to prove his generosity by being content to take less than he thinks' he deserves ; I want him to be generous enough to withdraw the motion. When you want to do a generous and gracious thing, do it handsomely.
Mr< GOURLEY. I will withdraw it, as- . suming, however, that the acting Minister of Railways and Canals will take into consideration the proposition, and endeavour to do justice to the maritime provinces.

Hear, hear.
Rideau canal-to complete Brasses' Point bridge, $2,750.
Where is that V

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is at Brewer's Mills.

The appropriation to complete this bridge was found insufficient. It is a steel superstructure. The contract price was $8,950 and the contract was awarded to the Dominion Bridge Company, who were the lowest tenderers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They had trouble with the piers.

I do not see auy item in the estimates for Poonamaiee crossing which was recommended to the department a couple of years ago. I had expected to see an item in the estimates for the purpose of doing this work and I hope that before the session is over there will be a grant made to the township of Elmsley and to the other township in Leeds county which are practically interested in this undertaking. It is money that they are in

justice entitled to. On account of the construction of the Rideau canal part of the highway has been overflowed. It has been reported by the superintendent of the canal and it should be attended to without further delay. It really does not require an item in the estimates because the general vote for the Rideau canal will cover it. A petition has been sent to the department in regard to another matter in connection with the township of Montague and a deputation has been here to see the Minister of Railways and Canals. The representations of that deputation were promised favourable consideration, and the deputation went home believing from the courteous manner in which they had been received they had virtually received a grant for the undertaking. X hope the hon. minister will see, his way clear to taking favourable action* in regard to these two matters. Damages have been caused, something in the line of those caused by the overflowing of the GrauX river in consequence of which money has been voted. As a result of the construction of the Poonamalee dam the parties living above it allege that the dam has been raised every year, that the overflow of water upon the land is greater every year and they claim that they are entitled to damages. It is a small amount that they require and their request is a legitimate one.
I will inquire into the matter.
Oh, yes, but inquiries have been made for a long time.
We will consider it. We must not make promises.
I should judge from that that there are to be further supplementary estimates.

We have some supplementary estimates to come down.
Welland canal-to complete dam and bridge at DunnvilJe, $12,000.
